vilka-materialgrupper-finns-det.back:
* Metals
* Ceramics
* Polymers

Glasses and elastomers are sometimes regarded as separate material groups, but they can otherwise be seen as subgroups of ceramics and polymers respectively. A combination of two or more materials is called a composite or hybrid and can sometimes also be seen as a material group of its own.

namn-minst-tva-olika-typer-av.front: Name at least two different types of atomic bonds and describe their characteristic properties.
namn-minst-tva-olika-typer-av.back:
* Covalent bond:
  - Strong
  - Directional
  - Ceramics, polymers
* Metallic bond:
  - Strong
  - Electron cloud → electrical and
thermal conduction
  - In metals
* Ionic bond
  - Strong
  - Bond between positive and
negative ions
  - Ceramics
* Van der Waals, hydrogen bond,
polar bonds
  - Weak
  - Between polymer chains

vad-ar-en-keram-och-vad-kannetecknar-dem.front: What is a ceramic and what characterises them?
vad-ar-en-keram-och-vad-kannetecknar-dem.back:
* Inorganic chemical compounds
between metal and non-metal
* E.g.: Al₂O₃, SiC, SiO₂
* Use covalent or ionic bonding
* Cement, concrete, brick, porcelain,
glass, technical ceramics

Properties:
* High melting temperature
* Chemically stable
* High stiffness, good wear resistance
* Brittle, cannot withstand tensile loading,
better in compressive loading
* Electrically and thermally
insulating

hur-tillverkas-vanligtvis-en-produkt.front: How is a product made of some kind of ceramic usually manufactured?
hur-tillverkas-vanligtvis-en-produkt.back:
* Ceramics are made from various
minerals
* Starting material in the form of clay
or powder
* Shaped into the form of the product
* Sintered (fired) at approx. 2/3 of
the ceramic's melting temperature

vad-ar-en-metall-och-vad-kannetecknar.front: What is a metal and what characterises them?
vad-ar-en-metall-och-vad-kannetecknar.back:
* Common metals
  - Steel
  - Aluminium
  - Cu, Mg, Ti, Ni
* Mostly used as an alloy
(mixture)
  - Steel = Fe + C
  - Bronze = Cu +Sn
  - Brass = Cu + Zn

Properties:
* Crystalline structure
* Medium to high melting temperature
* Electrically and thermally conductive
* High stiffness
* High yield strength (hardness)
* Not brittle
* High density
* Can be cast
* Can be shaped by plastic forming
methods: rolling, pressing
* Can be machined:
drilling, turning, milling

vad-ar-en-polymer-och-vad-kannetecknar.front: What is a polymer and what characterises them?
vad-ar-en-polymer-och-vad-kannetecknar.back:
* Organic materials consisting
of macromolecules
* Made from oil, but also from
other organic raw materials
* Plastic = polymer + additives

Properties:
* Low service temperature
* Relatively low stiffness and
yield strength
* Low density
* Electrically and thermally
insulating
* Easy to shape

vad-ar-en-komposit-och-vad-kannetecknar.front: What is a composite and what characterises them?
vad-ar-en-komposit-och-vad-kannetecknar.back:
* Combination of two or more
materials, e.g. plastic and carbon fibre
* Common fibres: carbon fibre, glass fibre,
aramid fibre
* The reinforcement can take different
forms: long fibres, short fibres,
particles
* Other examples:
  - Concrete = cement and stone
  - Cemented carbide = Co and WC

namn-minst-tva-olika-typer-av-2.front: Name at least two different types of manufacturing methods.
namn-minst-tva-olika-typer-av-2.back:
* Primary shaping
* Secondary shaping
* Joining
* Surface treatment

materialegenskaper-brukar-delas-upp-i.front: "Material properties" are usually divided into a number of subcategories; name at least three of them.
materialegenskaper-brukar-delas-upp-i.back:
* General properties
* Mechanical properties
* Electrical, magnetic and
optical properties
* Thermal properties
* Chemical properties
* Environment

ge-minst-tva-exempel-pa-mekaniska.front: Give at least two examples of mechanical properties.
ge-minst-tva-exempel-pa-mekaniska.back:
* Stiffness
  - How much a material
deforms under a given load.
* Yield strength
  - The load (stress) at which a
material deforms
permanently.
* Fracture toughness ($K_{1c}$)
  - The material's resistance to
crack growth.

ge-minst-tva-exempel-pa-elektriska.front: Give at least two examples of electrical, magnetic and optical properties.
ge-minst-tva-exempel-pa-elektriska.back:
* Electrical conductivity
* Electrical insulation
* Magnetic
* Transparent, reflection, colour

Depend on the interaction between
the electrons in the material

ge-minst-tva-exempel-pa-termiska.front: Give at least two examples of thermal properties.
ge-minst-tva-exempel-pa-termiska.back:
* Melting temperature
* Min and max
service temperature
* Thermal conduction
* Specific heat capacity
* Thermal expansion

ge-minst-tva-exempel-pa-kemiska.front: Give at least two examples of chemical properties.
ge-minst-tva-exempel-pa-kemiska.back:
* Corrosion (“rusts”)
* Oxidation (reacts with oxygen)
* Reactions in the service environment
* Toxic

ge-minst-tva-exempel-pa-miljoegenskaper.front: Give at least two examples of environmental properties.
ge-minst-tva-exempel-pa-miljoegenskaper.back:
* CO₂ footprint: amount of CO₂ that
is formed during production
* Embedded energy: amount of
energy required for
production
* Recyclable
* Other environmental impacts during
extraction, production,
product manufacture,
use and scrapping

adhesiv-forslitning.back: During wear, the materials bond together through atomic bonds, and material is torn away when the surfaces slide against each other. The two materials are welded together at points and torn apart.

abrasiv-forslitning.back: Wear that occurs when a hard material/medium cuts away the surface.

quiz-vad-ar-sant-for-atombindningar-tva.front: Which statements about atomic bonds are true?
quiz-vad-ar-sant-for-atombindningar-tva.back: Ceramics have covalent or ionic bonding. In the metallic bond the valence electrons are released and form an electron cloud, which gives electrical and thermal conduction. Hydrogen bonds, together with van der Waals bonds, belong to the weak bonds (e.g. between polymer chains), whereas ionic, covalent and metallic bonds are strong. Of the bond types in the lecture, it is the covalent bond that is described as directional.
options: Ceramic materials can have ionic bonds.
The type of bonding in metals gives electrical conductivity.
The strongest bonds are hydrogen bonds.
Ionic bonds and metallic bonds are directional.

quiz-vad-ar-sant-for-keramiska-material-.front: Which statements about ceramic materials are true?
quiz-vad-ar-sant-for-keramiska-material-.back: Ceramics are mostly crystalline, with glass as an amorphous exception, and they have covalent or ionic bonding. Strong bonds (a deep bond energy curve) give a high melting temperature. Ceramics are inorganic compounds between metal and non-metal, not compounds with organic materials, and despite being brittle they have good wear resistance. The quiz option "All ceramics are crystalline except glass" has been reworded to "mostly", as stated in the lecture.
options: Ceramics are mostly crystalline; glass is an exception and is amorphous.
The strong atomic bonding in ceramics gives a high melting temperature.
Ceramics are compounds between inorganic and organic materials.
Brittle ceramics have poor wear resistance.

quiz-mer-keramer-vad-ar-sant-tva-ratta-s.back: Ceramics are electrically and thermally insulating. They are brittle and withstand tensile loading poorly but compressive loading better. Ceramic products are not usually cast but are shaped from clay or powder and sintered at approx. 2/3 of the melting temperature. Glass is amorphous and softens and can be shaped only between 800 and 1200 °C, which is not a low temperature.
options: Ceramics are usually insulators.
When designing with ceramics, one should aim for compressive loading.
Ceramics are usually cast.
Glass is a ceramic with a low melting temperature.

quiz-vad-ar-sant-for-metaller-tva-ratta-.front: Which statements about metals are true?
quiz-vad-ar-sant-for-metaller-tva-ratta-.back: Brittle materials have low fracture toughness, and ceramics are brittle whereas metals are not. That metals can be cast is listed among the properties of metals in the lecture. Steel is iron and carbon (Fe + C), and other metals also corrode, e.g. magnesium, which forms a porous oxide layer and therefore has poorer corrosion protection. The quiz options are simplified: "higher fracture toughness than plastics and ceramics" is restricted to ceramics and "All metals can be cast" to "Metals can be cast", since the lecture text only supports that.
options: Metals generally have higher fracture toughness than ceramics.
Metals can be cast.
Steel is an alloy of iron and phosphorus.
The only metal that corrodes is steel.

quiz-vad-ar-sant-for-kompositer-tva-ratt.front: Which statements about composites are true?
quiz-vad-ar-sant-for-kompositer-tva-ratt.back: A composite is a combination of two or more materials, e.g. plastic and carbon fibre, and the reinforcement can be long fibres, short fibres or particles. The density of the composite depends on the volume fractions and densities of the constituent materials: according to the rule of mixtures, $\rho = f\rho_A + (1-f)\rho_B$, the densities are weighted by the volume fractions, so the density of the composite ends up between those of the constituent materials and not below both. Recycling of composites is described in the lecture as a challenge.
options: A composite usually consists of two different materials.
The reinforcement in a composite can consist of long fibres, short fibres or particles.
A composite always has a lower density than each of the constituent materials.
Composites are usually easy to recycle.

designbegransande-egenskap.back: A property that determines whether a material is suitable based on the design requirements. Example: for an aircraft, strength, stiffness and toughness are design-limiting; if any of them is too low, the aircraft cannot fly.

sex-materialfamiljer.front: Which of the following are families of their own in the course's division into six material families?
sex-materialfamiljer.back: The six families are metals (with alloys), ceramics, glasses, polymers, elastomers and hybrids (e.g. composites). In the coarser division into four groups, glasses are counted as ceramics and elastomers as polymers. Alloys belong to the metal family and thermoplastics are a subgroup of polymers, so neither of them is a family of its own.
options: Glasses
Elastomers
Alloys
Thermoplastics

komposit-kolfiber-begransningar.front: Which statements about carbon fibre composites are correct according to the course?
komposit-kolfiber-begransningar.back: Carbon fibre composites combine high strength with low weight and are used in e.g. aircraft, wind power, sport and medicine. They are sometimes called "the material of the future", but recycling is described in the course as a challenge. Price is an important limitation: in the course's chair example (BM 65), CFRP is dismissed as too expensive, and in the SpaceX example they switched from carbon fibre composite and cast titanium to stainless steel, partly for a lower cost per kilo and simpler manufacturing and repair. Low weight here means low density, so they have a lower density than steel, not a higher one.
options: They have high strength and low weight and are used e.g. in aircraft, wind power and sport.
Recycling is described as a challenge.
They are cheaper per kilo than stainless steel.
They have a higher density than steel.

vilka-ar-de-olika-stegen-i.front: What are the different steps in the materials selection process?
vilka-ar-de-olika-stegen-i.back:
1. Translate
2. Screen
3. Rank
4. Seek documentation

In addition to the four steps, one iterates: the material choice often needs to be refined in several steps before a good solution is found.

beskriv-vad-man-gor-i.front: Describe what is done in the materials selection step: "Translate".
beskriv-vad-man-gor-i.back:
Translate requirements on the component into requirements on the material:

* Function: states the main function of the material in
the component.
E.g. conduct heat, electrical insulation,
beam in bending that does not yield.
* Constraints: properties that must be met for the component to work.
E.g. service temperature, withstand
water, a certain fracture toughness
* Objectives: properties of the component that we want to optimise.
E.g. weight, price, environmental impact
* Free variables: variables of the component that we can change.
E.g. cross-section, material

beskriv-vad-man-gor-i-2.front: Describe what is done in the materials selection step: "Screen".
beskriv-vad-man-gor-i-2.back: Remove all materials that do not meet the constraints. (If we use these materials, the component will not work as we want.) Material properties that we use in the objective function should not be used in the screening either. (E.g. no constraint on density if the objective is low weight.)

beskriv-vad-man-gor-i-3.front: Describe what is done in the materials selection step: "Rank".
beskriv-vad-man-gor-i-3.back:
* Use function, objectives and free variables to determine the
material index.
* Material index = numerical value that describes how well a material meets the objectives!
* Use the material index to rank the materials.
E.g.: Young's modulus/price, Young's modulus^(1/2)/density

beskriv-vad-man-gor-i-4.front: Describe what is done in the materials selection step: "Seek documentation".
beskriv-vad-man-gor-i-4.back: Search the documentation (handbooks, articles, standards etc.) to see whether there is experience of the material in similar applications.

beskriv-vad-man-gor-i-5.front: What does it mean to iterate the material choice, and why is it important?
beskriv-vad-man-gor-i-5.back: The material choice often has to be refined and improved in several steps before a good solution is found. It is good to start with the material groups first and then narrow down. In CES (Granta EduPack) you start with Level 1 to find material groups and then move on to Levels 2 and 3.

vad-ar-ett-lastfall-och-varfor-ar-det.front: What is a load case and why is it important in the materials selection process?
vad-ar-ett-lastfall-och-varfor-ar-det.back:
* A load case is an isolated loading situation that the material can be subjected to.
* E.g.: A bar in compression/tension/torsion, a beam in bending/buckling or subjected to a distributed load, a pressure vessel subjected to pressure differences.
* The load case (together with what is to be optimised) determines which material index is appropriate. All cases of bending of a beam, for example, have the same influence of the material, so for the material choice one only needs to determine the type of load case.
* Examples for minimum weight: tie $\rho/E$ (stiffness) or $\rho/\sigma_y$ (strength), beam in bending $\rho/E^{1/2}$ or $\rho/\sigma_y^{2/3}$; choose materials with the lowest value.

beskriv-ingaende-vad-ett-materialindex.front: Describe in detail what a material index is and how it is used.
beskriv-ingaende-vad-ett-materialindex.back:
* A numerical value M that tells how efficient a material is in
a given load case and a given shape
* To determine the material index we need to know which property is to be optimised (e.g.: stiffness, price, weight) and the load case
* This is determined by the function, objectives and free variables from
the translation
* Material indices are used to rank materials in the materials selection

nar-ska-man-anvanda-materialindex-for.front: When should one use a material index for stiffness, as opposed to yield strength?
nar-ska-man-anvanda-materialindex-for.back:
* Use the material index for stiffness
if the deformation is
the limiting factor. (Constraint on max
deformation)
* Use the material index for
yield strength if load without yielding
is the limiting factor. (Constraint on max
stress)

quiz-materialval-vad-ar-sant-ett-ratt-sv.front: Materials selection: which statement is true?
quiz-materialval-vad-ar-sant-ett-ratt-sv.back: Material, shape and process interact: a specified process restricts the choice of material and shape. Minimal environmental impact can be an objective in materials selection and can be estimated with a quick eco audit, without a full life-cycle assessment. Screening only removes materials that do not meet the constraints and ranking decides which of the remaining ones is best, so a large number remaining is not a goal in itself. Free variables can be e.g. cross-section and material; in the course's heat sink example, the choice of material is the only free variable.
options: Materials selection is influenced by possible manufacturing methods.
Environmental impact cannot be included in materials selection but requires a life-cycle assessment.
The more materials remaining after screening, the better.
If the cross-section is not a free variable, a materials selection cannot be made.

quiz-materialval-vad-ar-sant-tva-ratta-s.front: Materials selection: which statements are true?
quiz-materialval-vad-ar-sant-tva-ratta-s.back: Screening removes all materials that do not meet the constraints, since the component would otherwise not work. The materials that remain meet the constraints and can be used; ranking with material indices then decides which one is best. Translation means that the requirements on the component are translated into function, constraints, objectives and free variables, and free variables are variables of the component that we can change, e.g. cross-section and material. The quiz option "All materials remaining after screening can be used to make the product" has been reworded so that it clearly refers to the constraints.
options: Materials that do not meet the constraints cannot be used in the component.
Materials remaining after screening meet the constraints and can therefore be used in the component.
Translation means translating the material requirements into Danish.
Free variables are things that are not necessary.

quiz-for-att-bestamma-materialindex-beho.front: What do you need to know to determine a material index?
quiz-for-att-bestamma-materialindex-beho.back: Which material index applies is determined by which property is to be optimised (the objective, e.g. low weight) and by the load case, i.e. by the function, objectives and free variables from the translation. Material data such as density, price, yield strength and Young's modulus are needed only when the index is calculated for the different materials, not to determine which index to use.
options: Load case
Objective
Density and price
Yield strength and Young's modulus

quiz-materialindex-vad-ar-ratt-2-ratta-s.front: Material indices: which statements are correct?
quiz-materialindex-vad-ar-ratt-2-ratta-s.back: Material indices rank materials by how well they meet the objective; the constraints are used in screening, not in ranking. An index can be a single property (e.g. just E if the performance is measured as the stiffness of a beam) or a combination such as $E/\rho$ or $\sigma_y/\rho$, so it does not need to contain the density. If there are several objectives, e.g. low weight and low price, several indices may be needed and the alternatives compared in a Pareto diagram.
options: Material indices are used in screening to remove the materials that do not meet the constraints.
A material index can contain one or more material properties.
Several material indices may be needed to arrive at a good material choice.
All material indices must contain the density of the material.

materialval-krav-eller-mal.front: Which of the following are constraints (and not objectives) in a translation?
materialval-krav-eller-mal.back: Constraints are properties that must be met for the component to work, e.g. service temperature, withstanding water or a certain fracture toughness. Objectives are properties of the component that we want to optimise (minimise or maximise), e.g. weight, price and environmental impact. The constraints are used in screening and the objectives in ranking.
options: Withstand water
A certain fracture toughness
Low weight
Low price

sallning-inget-krav-pa-malegenskap.front: If the objective is low weight, no constraint should be placed on density in the screening.
sallning-inget-krav-pa-malegenskap.back: Material properties included in the objective function should not be used in the screening. Density is instead handled in the ranking, via the material index (e.g. $\rho/\sigma_y$ for a light, strong tie).
options: True
False

materialindex-latt-stark-dragstang.front: Light, strong tie (must not yield): which material index should be minimised?
materialindex-latt-stark-dragstang.back: For a tie with minimum mass, $\rho/\sigma_y$ applies when strength (no yielding) is limiting and $\rho/E$ when stiffness is. $\rho/E^{1/2}$ and $\rho/\sigma_y^{2/3}$ are the indices for a light beam in bending (stiffness and strength respectively). Materials with the lowest value of the index are chosen, which is the same as the highest $\sigma_y/\rho$.
options: $\rho/\sigma_y$
$\rho/E$
$\rho/\sigma_y^{2/3}$

materialindex-latt-styv-balk.front: Light, stiff beam in bending (cross-sectional area free): which material index should be minimised?
materialindex-latt-styv-balk.back: For a light, stiff beam in bending the index is $\rho/E^{1/2}$ (minimised), i.e. choose materials with the highest $E^{1/2}/\rho$. $\rho/E$ applies to a stiff tie, $\rho/E^{1/3}$ to a stiff panel in bending and $\rho/\sigma_y^{2/3}$ to a beam where strength is limiting.
options: $\rho/E$
$\rho/\sigma_y^{2/3}$

harled-materialindex-dragstang.front: Derive the material index for a light, strong tie with given length L and load F.
harled-materialindex-dragstang.back:
Translation: function tie; objective minimum mass; constraints length L given and the tie must not fail (yield) under the load F; free variables the material and the cross-sectional area A.

1. The mass: $m = A L \rho$
2. The constraint: $F/A \le \sigma_y$, i.e. minimum area $A = F/\sigma_y$
3. Eliminate A: $m = F L \,(\rho/\sigma_y)$

F and L are given, so the mass is smallest for the material that has the lowest $\rho/\sigma_y$. That is the material index.

materialindex-lutning-bubbeldiagram.front: In a chart of $\log E$ against $\log \rho$, materials with the same value of $E^{1/2}/\rho$ lie on a line. What is the slope of the line?
materialindex-lutning-bubbeldiagram.back: If $E^{1/2}/\rho = C$, then $E = C^2\rho^2$, and taking logarithms $\log E = 2\log\rho + 2\log C$: a straight line with slope 2. All materials on the line have the same index value and are equally good; materials further up and to the left are better.

konceptdesign-materialdata.front: In the concept phase of design, detailed data for a single specific material are needed.
konceptdesign-materialdata.back: In concept design all materials are available and low-precision data are used, simple properties that are typical of each material group. In embodiment design a few materials are compared using more detailed data, and only in detailed design are well-specified data for one material and one process needed.
options: True
False

paretoyta-materialval.front: What is a Pareto surface (Pareto diagram) in materials selection, and when is it used?
paretoyta-materialval.back: It is used when there is a conflict between wishes (objectives), e.g. low weight and low price, and it is unclear which parameter is most important. A Pareto diagram shows which alternatives are the best compromises between the objectives.

materialindex-latt-stark-panel.front: Light, strong panel in bending (length and width given, thickness free): which material index should be minimised?
materialindex-latt-stark-panel.back: For minimum mass of a panel in bending, where strength is limiting and the thickness is the free variable, the index is $\rho/\sigma_y^{1/2}$; choose materials with the lowest value, i.e. the highest $\sigma_y^{1/2}/\rho$. $\rho/\sigma_y^{2/3}$ applies to a beam with free cross-sectional area, $\rho/\sigma_y$ to a tie and $\rho/E^{1/3}$ to a panel where stiffness is limiting.
options: $\rho/\sigma_y^{1/2}$
$\rho/\sigma_y^{2/3}$
$\rho/\sigma_y$

materialindex-billig-stark-balk.front: Cheap, strong beam in bending (length and load given, cross-sectional area free): which material index should be maximised?
materialindex-billig-stark-balk.back: When the objective is the lowest material cost instead of the lowest weight, the density $\rho$ is replaced by $C_m\rho$, where $C_m$ is the material cost per kg: the cost is the mass times the price per kilo. $\sigma_y^{2/3}/\rho$ is the index for a light, strong beam. $\sigma_y^{2/3}/C_m$ lacks the density, which is needed because $C_m$ is the price per kilo. $\sigma_y/(C_m\rho)$ applies to a cheap, strong tie.
options: $\sigma_y^{2/3}/(C_m\rho)$
$\sigma_y^{2/3}/\rho$
$\sigma_y^{2/3}/C_m$
$\sigma_y/(C_m\rho)$

materialindex-lutning-hallfast-balk.front: Materials for a light, strong beam are ranked with $\sigma_y^{2/3}/\rho$. What slope do lines of constant index value have in a chart of $\log\sigma_y$ against $\log\rho$?
materialindex-lutning-hallfast-balk.back: $\sigma_y^{2/3}/\rho = C$ gives $\sigma_y^{2/3} = C\rho$, so $\sigma_y = C^{3/2}\rho^{3/2}$ and $\log\sigma_y = 1.5\log\rho + 1.5\log C$: a straight line with slope 1.5. All materials on the line are equally good. Materials above the line have a higher $\sigma_y$ at the same density, i.e. a higher index value, and are better. The same derivation gives slope 2 for $E^{1/2}/\rho$ in an $E$–$\rho$ chart.

lastfall-identifiera-komponent.front: Which pairs of component and typical load case are correct?
lastfall-identifiera-komponent.back: In the translation, the function of the component is described as a typical load case, since the load case determines which material index applies. Ties carry tensile loads, beams bending moments, shafts torques and columns compressive loads. In the course exercise, the soft-drink can is a shell with internal pressure, the overhead power line a tie, and both the wind turbine blade and the shoe sole are beams in bending.
options: Soft-drink can: shell with internal pressure
Overhead power line: tie (pure tensile loading)
Wind turbine blade: beam in bending
Shoe sole: tie

materialindex-tryckkarl-cylinder.front: Light pressure vessel: a cylinder with given internal pressure and given radius, where the wall thickness is free, must not yield. Which material index should be maximised?
materialindex-tryckkarl-cylinder.back: In the course's index table for strength-limited design with minimum mass, $\sigma_y/\rho$ applies to a cylinder with internal pressure where the pressure and radius are given and the wall thickness is free. The wall is loaded in tension, and the index becomes the same as for a strong tie. $\sigma_y^{2/3}/\rho$ applies to a beam, $\sigma_y^{1/2}/\rho$ to a panel in bending and $E^{1/2}/\rho$ to a stiff beam.
options: $\sigma_y/\rho$
$\sigma_y^{2/3}/\rho$
$\sigma_y^{1/2}/\rho$

materialval-taltstang-oversattning.front: The tent poles for a mountain tent should be as light as possible. Do a translation and choose a material index.
materialval-taltstang-oversattning.back:
* **Function:** beam in bending, stiffness-limited
* **Constraints:** service temperature −30 to 50 °C, a certain fracture toughness (5 MPa√m), a certain yield strength (50 MPa), a certain Young's modulus (50 GPa), able to be formed into thin tubes
* **Objective:** low weight
* **Free variables:** cross-sectional area and material (metal or composite)

Material index: $M = E^{1/2}/\rho$, which is maximised (light, stiff beam). The constraints are used in screening and the objective in ranking. If the poles are also to be cheap, a second index is obtained, where $\rho$ is replaced by $C_m\rho$, and the conflict between objectives is handled with a Pareto diagram.

vad-ar-skillnaden-mellan-kristallin-och.front: What is the difference between a crystalline and an amorphous microstructure?
vad-ar-skillnaden-mellan-kristallin-och.back:
* Crystalline = ordered structure
  - Metals, ceramics, some polymers
* Amorphous = disordered structure
  - Polymers, glass

vad-ar-en-enhetscell-namn-minst-tva.front: What is a unit cell? Name at least two different types of unit cells.
vad-ar-en-enhetscell-namn-minst-tva.back:
* A small volume that can describe the whole crystal
* At each point there is an atom or molecule
* Six parameters: 3 lengths, 3 angles

E.g.: FCC (Face Centered Cubic), BCC (Body Centered Cubic), Triclinic, Simple Cubic, Close-Packed Hexagonal.

vad-kannetecknar-enhetscellen-fcc.back:
![The unit cells BCC, FCC and HCP with atomic packing factors 0.68, 0.74 and 0.74](/kort/materialteknik/enhetsceller-bcc-fcc-hcp.svg)

* Face centered cubic
* Face-centred cubic
* E.g.: Al, Cu, Ni, Au, Ag, austenitic stainless steel (austenite = FCC iron)
* Edge length a, angle 90 degrees
* Close-packed face diagonal
* Close-packed structure: atomic packing factor 0.74, stacking sequence ABCABC

vad-kannetecknar-enhetscellen-bcc.back:
![The unit cells BCC, FCC and HCP with atomic packing factors 0.68, 0.74 and 0.74](/kort/materialteknik/enhetsceller-bcc-fcc-hcp.svg)

* Body centered cubic
* Body-centred cubic
* E.g.: Fe (ferrite, $\alpha$-iron) from room temperature up to approx. 913 °C; above that the iron is FCC (austenite). Near the melting point (1394–1538 °C) the iron is BCC again, $\delta$-ferrite.
* Edge length a, angle 90 degrees
* Close-packed body diagonal
* Not a close-packed structure: atomic packing factor 0.68

det-finns-olika-typer-av-hal-i.front: There are different types of holes in crystal structures; what does this mean?
det-finns-olika-typer-av-hal-i.back:
* Between the atoms there are
cavities of different shape
and size
* Determine whether small atoms
can dissolve in
the material (e.g. C in Fe)

millerindex-beskriv-kortfattat-vad-det.front: Miller indices: Briefly describe what they are and how they are obtained.
millerindex-beskriv-kortfattat-vad-det.back:
![The planes (100), (110) and (111) marked in one cube each with the axes x, y and z](/kort/materialteknik/millerindex-plan.svg)

Miller indices describe the orientation of an atomic plane in the crystal (compare with the normal of the plane). The unit cell defines the coordinate system. This is how the indices of a plane are obtained:
1. Determine the intercepts of the plane with the coordinate axes
2. Invert
3. Convert to integers → Miller indices (hkl)

(hkl) = specific plane
{hkl} = family of planes

Directions are described by direction vectors in the same coordinate system, converted to integers (only the direction matters, not the length). In GLU 1 they are called "Miller indices for directions", also called direction indices:
[hkl] = specific direction
\<hkl> = family of directions

![The directions 100, 110 and 111 as arrows from the origin in one cube each](/kort/materialteknik/millerindex-riktningar.svg)

kristallin.back: Atoms or molecules arranged in an ordered structure.

quiz-kristaller-nar-man-beskriver-plan-o.front: Which notations denote a specific atomic plane or a specific direction in a crystal?
quiz-kristaller-nar-man-beskriver-plan-o.back: (hkl) denotes a specific plane and [hkl] a specific direction. {hkl} denotes a family of planes, and \<hkl> a family of directions.
options: (hkl)
[hkl]
{hkl}

quiz-kristallina-eller-amorfa-material-t.front: Crystalline and amorphous materials: which statements are true?
quiz-kristallina-eller-amorfa-material-t.back: Most metals are crystalline, with a regularly repeated pattern of atoms. Glass is amorphous (amorphous silica is the basis of most glasses), whereas ceramics otherwise are mostly crystalline. Polymers exist both as amorphous and as crystalline (some polymers). The quiz option "Metals are always crystalline" has been changed to "as a rule", since GLU 1 says "most metals".
options: Metals are as a rule crystalline.
Crystal glass is the only type of glass that is crystalline.
Polymers can be both amorphous and crystalline.
All ceramics except glass are amorphous.

quiz-kristaller-och-enhetsceller-tva-rat.front: Crystals and unit cells: which statements are true?
quiz-kristaller-och-enhetsceller-tva-rat.back: Close-packed planes are important because the slip planes, where dislocations move during plastic deformation, are the most close-packed planes. A unit cell is a model: the smallest volume that, repeated in space, describes the whole crystal. Amorphous materials lack an ordered structure (no long-range order) and are therefore not described by unit cells. FCC has an atomic packing factor of 0.74 and is close-packed, BCC has 0.68. The quiz option "Unit cells ... do not exist in reality" has been reworded according to the lecture's definition, which does not say so.
options: Close-packed atomic planes are important because that is where the material cracks.
The unit cell is a way of describing a crystal: the smallest volume that can describe the whole crystal.
To describe an amorphous material, special unit cells with more atoms are needed.
The FCC structure is close-packed but the BCC structure is not.

tatpackade-strukturer-fcc-hcp.front: Which structures are close-packed (atomic packing factor 0.74)?
tatpackade-strukturer-fcc-hcp.back:
![The unit cells BCC, FCC and HCP with atomic packing factors 0.68, 0.74 and 0.74](/kort/materialteknik/enhetsceller-bcc-fcc-hcp.svg)

FCC and HCP are both close-packed with an atomic packing factor of 0.74; they differ in the stacking sequence of the close-packed layers (ABCABC for FCC, ABAB for HCP). BCC has an atomic packing factor of 0.68 and an amorphous structure at most 0.64.
options: FCC
HCP
BCC
Amorphous structure

staplingsfoljd-abcabc.front: Close-packed atomic layers are stacked in the sequence ABCABC. Which structure does this give?
staplingsfoljd-abcabc.back: The stacking sequence ABCABC gives FCC and ABAB gives HCP; both are close-packed with an atomic packing factor of 0.74. BCC has an ABAB sequence of layers that are not fully close-packed (atomic packing factor 0.68), and an amorphous structure lacks regular stacking.
options: FCC
HCP
BCC
Amorphous structure

mikroskopi-lom-sem-tem.front: Which statements about microscopy of metals are correct?
mikroskopi-lom-sem-tem.back: The optical microscope is used to study the microstructure of cut, ground, polished and etched specimens. SEM gives a greater depth of field and much higher magnification and is used e.g. for fracture surfaces. In TEM only a small thin slice is examined, and there dislocations are visible.
options: In the transmission electron microscope (TEM), dislocations become visible because the lattice is locally distorted.
In the optical microscope, flat, polished and etched specimens are studied, where e.g. grain boundaries and pores are visible.
In TEM, whole components are examined without specimen preparation.
The scanning electron microscope (SEM) has a smaller depth of field and lower magnification than the optical microscope.

e-modul-enkristall-riktningsberoende.front: A single crystal has the same Young's modulus in all crystal directions.
e-modul-enkristall-riktningsberoende.back: Young's modulus is direction-dependent: a single crystal has different stiffness in different crystallographic directions. In a polycrystal with randomly oriented grains this evens out, so that the stiffness is isotropic on average.
options: True
False

millerindex-berakna-plan.front: A plane intersects the x-axis at 1/2, the y-axis at 1 and is parallel to the z-axis. What are the Miller indices of the plane?
millerindex-berakna-plan.back: The intercepts are 1/2, 1 and ∞ (parallel to z). Inverted, they become 2, 1 and 0, which are already integers, so the plane is (210). (120) is instead the plane that intersects the x-axis at 1 and the y-axis at 1/2, i.e. x and y swapped.

riktningsindex-berakna.front: A direction goes from the origin to the point (1/2, 1, 0) in the unit cell. What are its direction indices?
riktningsindex-berakna.back: The direction vector is (1/2, 1, 0). Directions are always converted to integers, since only the direction matters and not the length: multiply by 2 and the direction becomes [120]. Unlike Miller indices for planes, the components are not inverted.

millerindex-markerat-plan-110.front: What are the Miller indices of the marked plane? ![Cube with the axes x, y and z and a marked plane that intersects the x- and y-axes at 1 and is parallel to the z-axis](/kort/materialteknik/millerindex-fraga-plan-1.svg)
millerindex-markerat-plan-110.back: The plane intersects the x-axis at 1 and the y-axis at 1 and is parallel to the z-axis (intercept ∞). Inverted, this gives 1, 1 and 0, i.e. (110). (100) is the front face of the cube (x = 1), (111) intersects all three axes at 1, and (001) intersects only the z-axis (the top face of the cube).

millerindex-markerat-plan-111.front: The plane in the cube intersects the coordinate axes. What are its Miller indices? ![Cube with the axes x, y and z and a marked plane that intersects all three axes at 1](/kort/materialteknik/millerindex-fraga-plan-2.svg)
millerindex-markerat-plan-111.back: The plane intersects the x-, y- and z-axes at 1. Inverted, this gives 1, 1 and 1, i.e. (111). (110) is parallel to the z-axis, (100) is parallel to both the y- and z-axes and (001) to both the x- and y-axes.

riktningsindex-markerad-110.front: What are the direction indices of the marked direction? ![Cube with the axes x, y and z and an arrow from the origin to the corner (1, 1, 0)](/kort/materialteknik/millerindex-fraga-riktning-1.svg)
riktningsindex-markerad-110.back: The arrow goes from the origin to the corner (1, 1, 0), diagonally across the bottom face of the cube, so the direction is [110]. [111] is the body diagonal to (1, 1, 1), [100] runs along the x-axis and [011] is the diagonal in the back face of the cube x = 0, to (0, 1, 1).

vad-kannetecknar-enhetscellen-hcp.back:
![The unit cells BCC, FCC and HCP with atomic packing factors 0.68, 0.74 and 0.74](/kort/materialteknik/enhetsceller-bcc-fcc-hcp.svg)

* Hexagonal close packed (HCP, also CPH)
* Close-packed hexagonal
* Drawn as a hexagonal prism with an atom at each corner, one at the centre of each hexagonal face and three in the middle layer; the prism actually contains three unit cells
* Close-packed structure: atomic packing factor 0.74, the same as FCC, but the close-packed layers are stacked ABAB (FCC: ABCABC)
* Few slip systems, so HCP metals are more difficult to deform plastically than FCC metals
* E.g.: Mg, Ti, Zn

enhetscell-kanna-igen-bcc.front: Which of the unit cells is BCC (body-centred cubic)? ![Three unlabelled unit cells labelled A, B and C](/kort/materialteknik/enhetsceller-omarkerade.svg)
enhetscell-kanna-igen-bcc.back: C has an atom at each corner and one at the centre of the cube: body-centred cubic (BCC), where the atoms lie close together along the body diagonal. A has atoms at the corners and at the centre of each side face: face-centred cubic (FCC). B is the hexagonal prism: close-packed hexagonal (HCP). Easy to mix up: face-centred = FCC, body-centred = BCC.
options: A
B
C

millerindex-negativt-index.front: A plane intersects the x-axis at 1 and the y-axis at −1/2 and is parallel to the z-axis. What are the Miller indices of the plane?
millerindex-negativt-index.back: The intercepts are 1, −1/2 and ∞. Inverted, this gives 1, −2 and 0, which are already integers. A negative index is written with a bar over the digit: $(1\bar{2}0)$. $(120)$ has lost the minus sign, $(2\bar{1}0)$ is obtained if the x- and y-intercepts (1 and −1/2) are converted to integers without inverting them, and $(1\bar{1}0)$ is the plane that intersects the y-axis at −1.

millerindex-plan-genom-origo.front: How do you determine the Miller indices of a plane that passes through the origin?
millerindex-plan-genom-origo.back:
A plane through the origin intersects the axes at 0, and 1/0 cannot be inverted. Therefore move the plane one cell length along an axis (or, equivalently, move the origin to another corner of the unit cell) so that the plane does not pass through the origin. Then read off the intercepts, invert and convert to integers as usual. An intercept on the negative part of an axis gives a negative index, which is written with a bar over the digit.

Example: the diagonal plane that contains the x-axis (y = z = 0) and the opposite edge (y = z = 1). With the origin moved to the corner (0, 0, 1), the plane is parallel to the x-axis, intersects the y-axis at 1 and the z-axis at −1. Inverted, this gives 0, 1 and −1, i.e. $(01\bar{1})$.

millerindex-fran-index-till-plan.front: The plane $(213)$ in a cubic unit cell: where does it intersect the axes?
millerindex-fran-index-till-plan.back: Go backwards through the method: invert the indices 2, 1 and 3 to the intercepts 1/2, 1 and 1/3, and draw the plane through the three points. Check: if the intercepts are inverted again, this gives 2, 1 and 3, i.e. $(213)$. Simply taking the indices as intercepts (2, 1, 3) forgets the inversion, and the last two options have the axes swapped. An index of 0 means that the plane is parallel to that axis.

riktningsindex-mellan-tva-punkter.front: A direction goes from the point (0, 1, 1) to the point (1, 1/2, 0) in the unit cell. What are its direction indices?
riktningsindex-mellan-tva-punkter.back: A direction is moved so that it starts at the origin, which is the same as taking the end point minus the starting point: (1 − 0, 1/2 − 1, 0 − 1) = (1, −1/2, −1). Multiply by 2 to obtain integers: $[2\bar{1}\bar{2}]$. $[212]$ has lost the minus signs, $[210]$ is obtained if only the end point is taken, as if the direction started at the origin, and $[1\bar{2}\bar{1}]$ is obtained if the components are inverted as for a plane; directions are not inverted.

riktningsfamilj-111.front: Which directions in a cubic unit cell belong to the family of directions $\langle 111\rangle$?
riktningsfamilj-111.back:
![The directions 100, 110 and 111 as arrows from the origin in one cube each](/kort/materialteknik/millerindex-riktningar.svg)

$[hkl]$ is a specific direction and $\langle hkl\rangle$ a family of equivalent directions. $\langle 111\rangle$ are the body diagonals, e.g. $[111]$, $[\bar{1}11]$, $[1\bar{1}1]$ and $[11\bar{1}]$ (and the opposite directions). The edges of the cube belong to $\langle 100\rangle$, i.e. $[100]$, $[010]$ and $[001]$, and the face diagonals to $\langle 110\rangle$.
options: The body diagonals of the cube, from one corner through the centre of the cube to the opposite corner
The edges of the cube
The diagonals in the side faces of the cube

planfamilj-100.front: Which planes belong to the family of planes $\{100\}$ in a cubic unit cell?
planfamilj-100.back:
![The planes (100), (110) and (111) marked in one cube each with the axes x, y and z](/kort/materialteknik/millerindex-plan.svg)

$(hkl)$ is a specific plane and $\{hkl\}$ a family of equivalent planes. In a cube the side faces are equivalent, so $\{100\}$ comprises $(100)$, $(010)$ and $(001)$ and the corresponding planes with negative indices. The diagonal planes belong to $\{110\}$ and the planes that intersect all three axes at 1 to $\{111\}$.
options: The side faces of the cube: $(100)$, $(010)$ and $(001)$ and the parallel faces on the opposite side
The diagonal planes through two opposite edges, e.g. $(110)$
The planes that intersect all three axes at 1, e.g. $(111)$
Only the plane $(100)$

bcc-gitterparameter-atomradie.front: A metal with a BCC structure has the atomic radius r = 0.125 nm. What is the lattice parameter (edge length) a?
bcc-gitterparameter-atomradie.back: In BCC the atoms lie close together along the body diagonal, which is $a\sqrt{3}$ long and accommodates four atomic radii: $4r = a\sqrt{3}$, so $a = 4r/\sqrt{3} = 0.500/1.732 \approx 0.289$ nm. 0.354 nm is obtained with the FCC relation $4r = a\sqrt{2}$ (close-packed face diagonal), 0.250 nm if the atoms are assumed to lie close together along the edge ($a = 2r$) and 0.866 nm if one multiplies by $\sqrt{3}$ instead of dividing.
options: Approx. 0.289 nm
Approx. 0.354 nm
Approx. 0.250 nm
Approx. 0.866 nm

vad-ar-ett-fasdiagram-och-vad-anvands.front: What is a phase diagram and what is it used for?
vad-ar-ett-fasdiagram-och-vad-anvands.back: A phase diagram shows which phases are stable at which specific temperatures and compositions of the constituent metals in an alloy (also pressure etc.). It applies to slow processes, so that concentration differences can be evened out by means of diffusion = equilibrium is reached.

vad-ar-ferrit-och-nar-uppstar-det.front: What is Ferrite and when does it form?
vad-ar-ferrit-och-nar-uppstar-det.back:
![The unary phase diagram of iron with ferrite, austenite, delta ferrite, liquid and vapour](/kort/materialteknik/jarn-unart-fasdiagram.svg)

Ferrite ($\alpha$-iron) is iron with a BCC structure. In pure iron it is the stable phase up to approx. 913 °C. Ferrite has a low solubility of carbon.

Above approx. 1394 °C pure iron becomes BCC again, then called $\delta$-ferrite.

The figure follows the phase diagram in the Lab PM (912 °C); GLU 02 gives 913 °C.

vad-ar-austenit-och-nar-uppstar-det.front: What is Austenite and when does it form?
vad-ar-austenit-och-nar-uppstar-det.back:
![The unary phase diagram of iron with ferrite, austenite, delta ferrite, liquid and vapour](/kort/materialteknik/jarn-unart-fasdiagram.svg)

Austenite ($\gamma$-iron) is iron with an FCC structure. In pure iron it is the stable phase between approx. 913 °C and approx. 1394 °C. Austenite can dissolve up to approx. 2.1 % carbon.

The figure follows the phase diagram in the Lab PM (912 °C); GLU 02 gives 913 °C.

vad-ar-cementit-och-nar-uppstar-det.front: What is cementite and when does it form?
vad-ar-cementit-och-nar-uppstar-det.back: Cementite, Fe₃C, intermediate phase, 6.67 % C, very hard

metastabil.back: A state in a local energy minimum. To reach the state with the lowest energy (stable), an energy barrier must be overcome by supplying thermal energy. The phase has a higher Gibbs free energy but does not spontaneously transform into the more stable phase.

intermetall.back: An in-between phase in the phase diagram that consists only of metals (at least two). It has an exact or nearly stoichiometric composition, e.g. CuAl₂ in Al-Cu, and appears as a narrow single-phase region. In-between phases with a wider composition range are called intermediate phases.

eutektikum.back:
A microconstituent consisting of two phases. The eutectic forms at constant temperature
and concentration through a three-phase reaction in which a liquid phase L forms two solid phases: L → alpha + beta

ja-nej-perlit-bildas-vid-en-eutektisk.front: Pearlite forms in a eutectic reaction from the melt.
ja-nej-perlit-bildas-vid-en-eutektisk.back:
![Simplified Fe–C diagram for steel with the eutectoid point S at approx. 0.8 % C and approx. 723 °C](/kort/materialteknik/fe-c-stalhornet.svg)

Pearlite forms in the eutectoid reaction, which takes place in the solid state: austenite transforms into ferrite and cementite at approx. 0.8 % C and approx. 723 °C. A eutectic reaction starts from the melt ($L \to \alpha + \beta$); in Fe-C it takes place at 4.3 % C and 1147 °C and is relevant for cast iron.
options: True
False

loslighetsgrans.back: The highest concentration of a substance that can be dissolved in a phase.

strukturbestandsdel.back:
A distinguishable part of the material that consists of one or more phases and can be regarded as a unit in
some way. Can be a phase, eutectic or eutectoid.

fas.back: A part of the material with homogeneous physical and chemical properties

quiz-vad-galler-for-gibbs-fria-energi-tv.front: Which statements about Gibbs free energy are true?
quiz-vad-galler-for-gibbs-fria-energi-tv.back: Gibbs free energy is enthalpy minus temperature times entropy, $G = H - TS$. Enthalpy is energy stored in the material, e.g. elastic straining of the atomic bonds, and entropy is linked to disorder, so increased disorder lowers G. The concept applies to all phases, including liquid and gas (ice, water and water vapour are different phases), and a material strives towards the phase that has the lowest G at the current temperature.
options: Gibbs free energy is the sum of the kinetic energy of the atoms.
The potential energy of the atomic bonds contributes to Gibbs free energy.
Gibbs free energy decreases with increasing disorder in the material.
Gibbs free energy applies only to solid materials.

quiz-jamvikt-och-stabilitet-tva-ratt.front: Equilibrium and stability: which statements are true?
quiz-jamvikt-och-stabilitet-tva-ratt.back: The stable phase is the one with the lowest Gibbs free energy. A metastable phase does not have the lowest G but requires activation energy (usually heat) to transform into the stable phase, and can therefore persist, e.g. martensite in hardened steel or the supersaturated $\alpha$ phase in quenched aluminium. An unstable phase also has a free energy; sooner or later it transforms into the stable phase, at a rate that can be limited by diffusion.
options: Gibbs free energy can be used to determine whether the material is in a stable state.
Gibbs free energy can be used to determine whether the material is in a metastable state.
Gibbs free energy is undefined when the material is in an unstable state.
A material can only be in a metastable state for a short time (a few seconds to a few days depending on temperature).

quiz-fasdiagram-tva-ratt.front: Phase diagrams: which statements are true?
quiz-fasdiagram-tva-ratt.back: In a binary phase diagram the single-phase regions are separated by two-phase regions, even between the narrow lines for stoichiometric phases. The phase diagram shows which phases are stable (have the lowest Gibbs free energy) at a given temperature and composition; time is not included, and the diagram applies to processes so slow that equilibrium is reached. A metastable phase such as martensite is therefore not found in the phase diagram. The quiz options ("Two single-phase regions always have a two-phase region between them", "A phase diagram shows only stable phases") have been reworded without "always" and "only", which the lectures do not use; the first has also been narrowed to binary phase diagrams, since the single-phase regions in a unary phase diagram (a single substance, e.g. iron) are separated only by transformation temperatures.
options: In a binary phase diagram there are two-phase regions between the single-phase regions.
A phase diagram shows how stable phases change with time.
A phase diagram shows which phases are stable at a given temperature and composition.
Metastable phases are usually marked in red in the phase diagram.

quiz-stals-fasdiagram-vad-ar-sant-tva-ra.front: The phase diagram of steel: which statements are true?
quiz-stals-fasdiagram-vad-ar-sant-tva-ra.back:
![Simplified Fe–C diagram for steel with phases and microconstituents around the eutectoid point](/kort/materialteknik/fe-c-stalhornet.svg)

The phases in the Fe-C diagram are ferrite, austenite and cementite; martensite is a metastable phase that forms on rapid cooling and is not found in the phase diagram. Cementite (Fe₃C) contains 6.67 % C, more than austenite (up to 2.1 %) and ferrite (low solubility). Pearlite is a microconstituent of ferrite and cementite that forms at the eutectoid point (approx. 0.8 % C), and its fraction can be calculated with the lever rule. Austenite is a separate phase with a different crystal structure (FCC iron) from ferrite (BCC iron). The quiz option "If carbon is dissolved in ferrite, austenite forms" has been reworded, since it is not unambiguously false: at e.g. 850 °C pure iron is ferrite but a steel with 0.3 % C is austenite.
options: Cementite, ferrite and martensite are all phases in the phase diagram.
Cementite is the phase in steel that contains the most carbon.
Pearlite is not a phase, but its carbon content and fraction can still be determined from the phase diagram.
Austenite is ferrite with dissolved carbon.

quiz-eutektiska-och-eutektoida-reaktione.front: Eutectic and eutectoid reactions: which statements are true?
quiz-eutektiska-och-eutektoida-reaktione.back: Three-phase reactions take place at constant temperature and concentration: the eutectic $L \to \alpha + \beta$ from the melt and the eutectoid $\gamma \to \alpha + \beta$ in the solid state. Pearlite forms eutectoidally from austenite, not from the melt. In a phase transformation on cooling, heat is released, so no heat needs to be supplied, but the reaction requires diffusion of carbon; on rapid cooling the carbon does not have time to diffuse and martensite then forms instead of pearlite.
options: In both eutectic and eutectoid reactions the temperature is constant.
Pearlite forms in a eutectic reaction from the melt.
Eutectoid reactions require heat to be supplied, otherwise nothing happens.
Eutectoid reactions require diffusion; without diffusion no eutectoid reaction takes place.

quiz-fasdiagram-vad-ar-sant-tva-ratta-sv.front: Phase diagrams: which statements about solubility and the lever rule are true?
quiz-fasdiagram-vad-ar-sant-tva-ratta-sv.back:
![The Pb–Sn phase diagram with the eutectic point at 61.9 % Sn and 183 °C](/kort/materialteknik/pb-sn-fasdiagram.svg)

With unlimited solubility, e.g. Cu-Ni, there is a single solid phase at all compositions below the solidus line. The solubility limit is the maximum concentration of a substance that can be dissolved in another, and it depends on the temperature (in Pb-Sn the solubility of Sn in Pb is greatest, 18.3 %, at 183 °C). The lever rule applies in all two-phase regions, including where liquid and solid phase coexist.
options: A phase diagram with unlimited solubility has only one solid phase.
The solubility limit usually changes with temperature.
The lever rule applies only to phases in the solid state.
The solubility limit tells how difficult it is to alloy a metal.

havstang-pbsn-40-strukturbestandsdelar.front: Pb-40 % Sn cools slowly from the melt. What fractions are primary $\alpha$ and eutectic, respectively, just below 183 °C? ![The Pb–Sn phase diagram with 18.3 %, 61.9 % and 97.8 % Sn at 183 °C](/kort/materialteknik/pb-sn-fasdiagram.svg)
havstang-pbsn-40-strukturbestandsdelar.back: Just above 183 °C the alloy consists of Pb-rich phase $\alpha$ (18.3 % Sn) and liquid of eutectic composition (61.9 % Sn). The lever rule gives the fraction of primary $\alpha$ $= \frac{61.9-40}{61.9-18.3} = \frac{21.9}{43.6} \approx 0.50$. The remainder, approx. 50 %, is liquid that solidifies into eutectic at 183 °C. 73 % is the fraction of the phase $\alpha$ in total (primary $\alpha$ plus $\alpha$ in the eutectic), not of the microconstituent primary $\alpha$.
options: Approx. 50 % primary $\alpha$ and 50 % eutectic
Approx. 40 % primary $\alpha$ and 60 % eutectic
Approx. 73 % primary $\alpha$ and 27 % eutectic
100 % eutectic

havstang-pbsn-40-faser.front: Pb-40 % Sn just below 183 °C: what are the fractions of the phases $\alpha$ and $\beta$? ![The Pb–Sn phase diagram with 18.3 %, 61.9 % and 97.8 % Sn at 183 °C](/kort/materialteknik/pb-sn-fasdiagram.svg)
havstang-pbsn-40-faser.back: Just below 183 °C there are two phases: $\alpha$ with 18.3 % Sn and $\beta$ with 97.8 % Sn (the solubility of Pb in Sn is only 2.2 %). The lever rule gives the fraction of $\alpha$ $= \frac{97.8-40}{97.8-18.3} = \frac{57.8}{79.5} \approx 0.73$ and the fraction of $\beta \approx 0.27$. The phase fractions differ from the fractions of the microconstituents (primary $\alpha$ and eutectic, approx. 50 % each).
options: Approx. 73 % $\alpha$ and 27 % $\beta$
Approx. 50 % $\alpha$ and 50 % $\beta$
Approx. 60 % $\alpha$ and 40 % $\beta$
Approx. 27 % $\alpha$ and 73 % $\beta$

havstangsregeln-metod.front: How do you use the lever rule in a two-phase region?
havstangsregeln-metod.back:
1. Draw a horizontal line (tie line) at the current temperature through the alloy composition $C$ out to the boundaries of the two-phase region.
2. Read off the concentrations of the phases $C_\alpha$ and $C_\beta$ at the boundaries.
3. The fraction of a phase is the opposite lever arm divided by the whole lever:

$f_\alpha = \dfrac{C_\beta - C}{C_\beta - C_\alpha}, \qquad f_\beta = \dfrac{C - C_\alpha}{C_\beta - C_\alpha}$

This is linear interpolation: at $C = C_\alpha$ the fraction of $\beta$ is 0 % and at $C = C_\beta$ 100 %.

segring.back: Concentration differences within the grains that arise during solidification, because diffusion is too limited to even out the composition. Almost always occurs in casting in practice.

karnbildning.back: The formation of new crystals in the melt, which then grow. Nucleation occurs more easily on solid particles and surfaces, and in casting small particles are therefore added to obtain a finer grain structure. The grains grow until they meet and form the grain structure and grain boundaries of the material.

ren-metall-stelningstemperatur.front: A pure metal solidifies over a temperature range.
ren-metall-stelningstemperatur.back: A pure metal has a distinct melting temperature. When it solidifies, heat is released, and the cooling curve has a plateau until everything has solidified. An alloy, on the other hand, usually solidifies over a temperature range, where melt and solid crystals are in equilibrium in a two-phase region.
options: True
False

eutektoidiskt-stal-faser-strukturbestand.front: A eutectoid steel (approx. 0.8 % C) that has cooled slowly consists of two phases but only one microconstituent.
eutektoidiskt-stal-faser-strukturbestand.back:
![Simplified Fe–C diagram for steel with phases and microconstituents around the eutectoid point](/kort/materialteknik/fe-c-stalhornet.svg)

Below the eutectoid temperature the steel consists of the phases ferrite and cementite, but they occur together as the single microconstituent pearlite (lamellae of ferrite and cementite). Above the eutectoid temperature the steel is a single phase, austenite, which is also the only microconstituent.
options: True
False

undereutektoidiskt-stal-strukturbestands.front: Which microconstituents does a hypoeutectoid steel (below approx. 0.8 % C) have after slow cooling?
undereutektoidiskt-stal-strukturbestands.back:
![Simplified Fe–C diagram for steel with phases and microconstituents around the eutectoid point](/kort/materialteknik/fe-c-stalhornet.svg)

On slow cooling, primary (proeutectoid) ferrite forms first, and at the eutectoid temperature the rest of the austenite transforms into pearlite. Only pearlite is obtained at approx. 0.8 % C, and pearlite with cementite at the boundaries between the pearlite regions in hypereutectoid steels. Martensite forms only on rapid cooling from the austenite region.
options: Primary ferrite and pearlite
Pearlite and cementite
Only pearlite
Martensite

tvafasomrade-fasernas-sammansattning.front: In a two-phase region, both phases have the same composition as the alloy.
tvafasomrade-fasernas-sammansattning.back: In a two-phase region the concentrations of the phases are read off at the boundaries of the region, along a horizontal line at the current temperature, and they differ from the composition of the alloy. Only in a single-phase region does the phase have the same concentration as the alloy.
options: True
False

stelning-pbsn-40.front: Describe how a Pb-40 % Sn alloy solidifies and cools slowly from the melt to room temperature.
stelning-pbsn-40.back:
![The Pb–Sn phase diagram with the eutectic point at 61.9 % Sn and 183 °C](/kort/materialteknik/pb-sn-fasdiagram.svg)

* Approx. 240 to 184 °C: Pb-rich phase ($\alpha$) forms gradually in equilibrium with the liquid, up to approx. 50 %.
* 183 °C: the remaining liquid, which then has eutectic composition (61.9 % Sn), solidifies into eutectic, a finely dispersed mixture of $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
* Below 183 °C: the solubility of Sn in Pb decreases, so Sn-rich phase ($\beta$) separates out as precipitates in the Pb-rich phase.

The result is primary $\alpha$ (with $\beta$ precipitates) and eutectic, roughly half of each.

jarn-fas-vid-1000.front: Which phase is stable in pure iron at 1000 °C?
jarn-fas-vid-1000.back:
![The unary phase diagram of iron with ferrite, austenite, delta ferrite, liquid and vapour](/kort/materialteknik/jarn-unart-fasdiagram.svg)

In pure iron, austenite is stable between approx. 912 °C and 1394 °C, so at 1000 °C the iron is austenitic (FCC). Ferrite ($\alpha$) is stable below approx. 912 °C, $\delta$-ferrite between 1394 °C and the melting point 1538 °C. GLU 02 gives the ferrite–austenite transformation as 913 °C, the phase diagram in the Lab PM 912 °C.
options: Austenite ($\gamma$-iron, FCC)
Ferrite ($\alpha$-iron, BCC)
$\delta$-ferrite (BCC)
Liquid

jarn-bcc-rumstemp-och-nara-smaltpunkten.front: Pure iron has a BCC structure both at room temperature and just below the melting point.
jarn-bcc-rumstemp-och-nara-smaltpunkten.back:
![The unary phase diagram of iron with ferrite, austenite, delta ferrite, liquid and vapour](/kort/materialteknik/jarn-unart-fasdiagram.svg)

True. At room temperature pure iron is ferrite ($\alpha$-iron, BCC). Between 1394 °C and the melting point 1538 °C it is $\delta$-ferrite, which is also BCC. In between, from approx. 912 °C to 1394 °C, the iron is austenite (FCC).
options: True
False

pbsn-40-vid-200.front: A Pb–Sn alloy with 40 % Sn is held at 200 °C. Which phases are present? ![The Pb–Sn phase diagram with single-phase and two-phase regions around the eutectic line at 183 °C](/kort/materialteknik/pb-sn-fasdiagram.svg)
pbsn-40-vid-200.back: The point 40 % Sn, 200 °C lies above the eutectic line at 183 °C but below the liquidus line (which at 40 % Sn lies at approx. 240 °C), i.e. in the two-phase region $\alpha$ + L. $\alpha$ + $\beta$ are present only below 183 °C, and a pure $\alpha$ region exists at 200 °C only for low Sn contents.
options: Pb-rich solid phase ($\alpha$) and liquid (L)
Only liquid (L)
$\alpha$ and $\beta$
Only $\alpha$

stal-03-primar-ferrit.front: A steel with 0.3 % C cools slowly from the austenite region. What happens between approx. 820 °C and approx. 723 °C?
stal-03-primar-ferrit.back:
![Simplified Fe–C diagram for steel with phases and microconstituents around the eutectoid point](/kort/materialteknik/fe-c-stalhornet.svg)

Between approx. 820 °C and 723 °C the steel lies in the two-phase region $\alpha$ + $\gamma$, where primary ferrite forms. At 723 °C the remaining austenite transforms eutectoidally into pearlite, so the steel finally consists of primary ferrite and pearlite. Cementite at the boundaries between the pearlite regions belongs to hypereutectoid steels, and martensite forms only on rapid cooling.
options: Primary (proeutectoid) ferrite forms from the austenite.
The eutectoid reaction forms pearlite.
Cementite precipitates at the grain boundaries.
The austenite transforms into martensite.

binart-fasdiagram.back: A phase diagram for a system of two substances (components), e.g. Cu–Ni or Pb–Sn. It shows which phases are stable at equilibrium at different temperatures (the y-axis) and compositions (the x-axis, the content of one of the substances). The single-phase regions are separated by two-phase regions. In Cu–Ni, with unlimited solubility, there is a single solid phase. In Pb–Sn, with limited solubility, there are two solid phases and a eutectic point.

eutektisk-sammansattning-lagst-smalttemp.front: In the Pb–Sn system, the alloy of eutectic composition has a lower melting temperature than both pure lead and pure tin.
eutektisk-sammansattning-lagst-smalttemp.back:
![The Pb–Sn phase diagram with the eutectic point at 61.9 % Sn and 183 °C](/kort/materialteknik/pb-sn-fasdiagram.svg)

True. The liquidus lines fall from pure Pb (327 °C) and pure Sn (232 °C) and meet at the eutectic point at 61.9 % Sn and 183 °C, the lowest temperature at which liquid exists in the system. A melt of eutectic composition has no solidification range but solidifies at a single temperature into eutectic. The same pattern is found in Al–Si: the eutectic temperature, approx. 577 °C (at 12.6 % Si), is lower than the melting points of both Al (660 °C) and Si (1414 °C).
options: True
False

avsvalningskurvor-former.front: What does the cooling curve look like when a pure metal, an alloy that solidifies as a single phase, and an alloy with a primary phase and eutectic solidify?
avsvalningskurvor-former.back:
When a phase forms, heat is released, which slows down the cooling. In a single-phase region the curve is governed only by heat conduction.

* **Pure metal (and eutectic composition):** a plateau (thermal arrest) at a single temperature until everything has solidified.
* **Alloy that solidifies as a single phase** (the two-phase region liquid + solid phase): a kink where solidification starts (the liquidus line), a flatter curve through the solidification range and a new kink where solidification is complete (the solidus line).
* **Alloy between a primary phase and eutectic:** first a kink when the primary phase starts to form, then a plateau at the eutectic temperature when the rest of the liquid solidifies into eutectic.

![Three cooling curves, temperature against time: pure metal with a plateau, alloy with kinks at liquidus and solidus, alloy with a kink at liquidus and a plateau at the eutectic temperature](/kort/materialteknik/avsvalningskurvor.svg)

avsvalningskurva-pbsn-knick-plata.front: A Pb–Sn alloy cools slowly from the melt. The cooling curve first has a kink and then a plateau at 183 °C. What composition can the alloy have? ![The Pb–Sn phase diagram with 18.3 %, 61.9 % and 97.8 % Sn at 183 °C](/kort/materialteknik/pb-sn-fasdiagram.svg)
avsvalningskurva-pbsn-knick-plata.back: The kink shows that primary $\alpha$ starts to form when the temperature reaches the liquidus line. The plateau at 183 °C is the eutectic reaction, in which the rest of the liquid solidifies into eutectic at constant temperature. Pb–61.9 % Sn has eutectic composition and gives only a plateau. Pb–10 % Sn solidifies completely into one phase ($\alpha$) over a temperature range and never reaches the eutectic line, so the curve has kinks but no plateau. Pure Sn gives only a plateau, at the melting point of tin.
options: Pb–30 % Sn
Pb–61.9 % Sn
Pb–10 % Sn
Pure Sn

havstang-stal-035-andel-perlit.front: A steel with 0.35 % C cools slowly from the austenite region. Approximately what fractions of pearlite and primary ferrite does it get? (Pearlite forms from austenite with 0.8 % C; the carbon content of the ferrite can be neglected.)
havstang-stal-035-andel-perlit.back:
![Simplified Fe–C diagram for steel with phases and microconstituents around the eutectoid point](/kort/materialteknik/fe-c-stalhornet.svg)

Just above the eutectoid temperature (approx. 723 °C) the steel consists of primary ferrite and austenite with 0.8 % C, and all of that austenite becomes pearlite in the eutectoid reaction. The lever rule between ferrite (≈ 0 % C) and austenite (0.8 % C): fraction of pearlite $= \dfrac{0.35 - 0}{0.8 - 0} \approx 0.44$, the remainder, approx. 56 %, is primary ferrite. 56 % pearlite is obtained if the lever arms are swapped, 35 % if the carbon content is taken as the fraction, and 100 % pearlite applies only at approx. 0.8 % C.
options: Approx. 44 % pearlite and 56 % primary ferrite
Approx. 56 % pearlite and 44 % primary ferrite
Approx. 35 % pearlite and 65 % primary ferrite
100 % pearlite

stal-austenit-blir-perlit-andel.front: The fraction of pearlite in a hypoeutectoid steel after slow cooling is equal to the fraction of austenite just above the eutectoid temperature.
stal-austenit-blir-perlit-andel.back: True. In the two-phase region ferrite + austenite, primary ferrite forms, and at the eutectoid temperature the remaining austenite, which then has approx. 0.8 % C, transforms into pearlite. The fraction of austenite just above the eutectoid temperature, calculated with the lever rule, thus becomes the fraction of pearlite. Higher up in the two-phase region the austenite has a lower carbon content and the fraction of austenite is larger; there the carbon content of the austenite is read off at the boundary of the two-phase region at the current temperature.
options: True
False

fe-c-andel-perlit-overeutektoid.front: A steel with 1.3 % C cools slowly. Approximately what fractions of pearlite and cementite does it have at room temperature? (Pearlite 0.8 % C, cementite 6.67 % C.)
fe-c-andel-perlit-overeutektoid.back: A hypereutectoid steel consists of pearlite and cementite, which lies at the boundaries between the pearlite regions. The lever rule between pearlite (0.8 % C) and cementite (6.67 % C) gives the fraction of pearlite $= \dfrac{6.67 - 1.3}{6.67 - 0.8} = \dfrac{5.37}{5.87} \approx 0.91$. 62 % is obtained from $0.8/1.3$, and 81 % $= (6.67 - 1.3)/6.67$ is the fraction of the phase ferrite (lever between ferrite and cementite), not of the microconstituent pearlite.
options: Approx. 91 % pearlite and 9 % cementite
Approx. 62 % pearlite and 38 % cementite
Approx. 81 % pearlite and 19 % cementite
100 % pearlite

fe-c-eutektisk-reaktion.front: What forms when a melt with 4.3 % C cools through the eutectic point in the Fe–C diagram (approx. 1147 °C)?
fe-c-eutektisk-reaktion.back: The eutectic reaction in Fe–C is liquid → austenite + cementite ($L \to \gamma + \text{Fe}_3\text{C}$) at 4.3 % C and approx. 1147 °C. It is exploited in the casting of cast iron (2–4 % C). Pearlite (ferrite + cementite) instead forms in the eutectoid reaction from austenite, at approx. 0.8 % C and 723 °C. Martensite forms only on rapid cooling of austenite, and a single phase is not a eutectic.
options: Austenite and cementite, in a eutectic
Ferrite and cementite, i.e. pearlite
Martensite
Only austenite

pbsn-stelning-sammansattning-andre.front: A Pb–30 % Sn alloy cools slowly through the two-phase region $\alpha$ + L down towards 183 °C. What happens?
pbsn-stelning-sammansattning-andre.back:
![The Pb–Sn phase diagram with single-phase and two-phase regions around the eutectic line at 183 °C](/kort/materialteknik/pb-sn-fasdiagram.svg)

In a two-phase region the concentrations of the phases are read off at the boundaries of the region, along a horizontal line at the current temperature: that of the liquid on the liquidus line and that of the solid phase on the solidus line. As a Sn-poorer solid phase separates out, the liquid is enriched in Sn, and the fraction of $\alpha$ increases according to the lever rule. Just above 183 °C, $\frac{30-18.3}{61.9-18.3} \approx 0.27$ remains, i.e. approx. 27 % liquid of eutectic composition, which solidifies into eutectic.
options: The Sn content of the liquid follows the liquidus line and increases towards 61.9 % Sn.
The fraction of the solid Pb-rich phase ($\alpha$) increases.
The liquid has the composition of the alloy, 30 % Sn, the whole time.
The fraction of liquid is constant until 183 °C is reached.

havstang-pbsn-70-strukturbestandsdelar.front: Pb–70 % Sn cools slowly from the melt. Approximately what fractions of primary $\beta$ and eutectic, respectively, are present just below 183 °C? ![The Pb–Sn phase diagram with 18.3 %, 61.9 % and 97.8 % Sn at 183 °C](/kort/materialteknik/pb-sn-fasdiagram.svg)
havstang-pbsn-70-strukturbestandsdelar.back: The alloy lies on the Sn side of the eutectic point, so the Sn-rich phase $\beta$ (97.8 % Sn at 183 °C) forms first. Just above 183 °C the fraction of primary $\beta$ $= \dfrac{70-61.9}{97.8-61.9} = \dfrac{8.1}{35.9} \approx 0.23$. The remainder, approx. 77 %, is liquid of eutectic composition, which solidifies into eutectic at 183 °C.
options: Approx. 23 % primary $\beta$ and 77 % eutectic
Approx. 77 % primary $\beta$ and 23 % eutectic
Approx. 70 % primary $\beta$ and 30 % eutectic
100 % eutectic

pbsn-strukturbestandsdelar-under-eutekti.front: When a Pb–Sn alloy of primary $\alpha$ and eutectic cools further from 183 °C to room temperature, the fraction of eutectic does not change, but Sn-rich $\beta$ separates out in the Pb-rich phase.
pbsn-strukturbestandsdelar-under-eutekti.back: True. The microconstituents, primary $\alpha$ and eutectic, form during solidification and remain on further cooling. Below 183 °C the solubility of Sn in Pb decreases, so Sn-rich phase $\beta$ forms as precipitates in the Pb-rich phase. The fractions of the phases $\alpha$ and $\beta$ thus change somewhat, whereas the fractions of the microconstituents remain the same.
options: True
False

havstang-faser-i-eutektikum.front: What fraction of the eutectic itself in Pb–Sn is $\beta$ phase just below 183 °C, when the eutectic has just formed? ![The Pb–Sn phase diagram with 18.3 %, 61.9 % and 97.8 % Sn at 183 °C](/kort/materialteknik/pb-sn-fasdiagram.svg)
havstang-faser-i-eutektikum.back: The eutectic has the composition 61.9 % Sn and consists of $\alpha$ (18.3 % Sn) and $\beta$ (97.8 % Sn). The lever rule with the eutectic's own composition gives, just below 183 °C, the fraction $\beta = \dfrac{61.9 - 18.3}{97.8 - 18.3} = \dfrac{43.6}{79.5} \approx 0.55$ and the fraction $\alpha \approx 0.45$. 62 % is the Sn content of the eutectic, not the fraction of $\beta$ at 183 °C, and 27 % is the fraction of $\beta$ in the whole alloy Pb–40 % Sn just below 183 °C. On further slow cooling the phases become almost pure Pb and pure Sn, and the fraction of $\beta$ in the eutectic then approaches its Sn content, approx. 62 %.
options: Approx. 55 %
Approx. 62 %
Approx. 27 %
Approx. 50 %

al-cu-max-halt-utskiljningshardning.front: Approximately what is the highest Cu content an Al–Cu alloy can have if all the Cu is to be dissolvable in $\alpha$ during solution heat treatment? ![The Al corner of the Al–Cu phase diagram with the aluminium phase (Al), the eutectic line at 548 °C and the phase θ = CuAl₂](/kort/materialteknik/al-cu-alhornet.svg)
al-cu-max-halt-utskiljningshardning.back: Solution heat treatment requires the alloy to become a single phase, $\alpha$, so that all the Cu is dissolved before quenching. The solubility of Cu in $\alpha$ is greatest at the eutectic temperature 548 °C, where the boundary of the $\alpha$ region meets the eutectic line, at just under 6 % Cu. At a higher Cu content, eutectic ($\alpha$ + $\theta$) forms during solidification, and there is no temperature at which all the Cu is dissolved in solid $\alpha$. Approx. 33 % is the eutectic composition, approx. 54 % is the phase $\theta$ (CuAl₂), and approx. 1 % is the solubility at a considerably lower temperature, not the greatest solubility.
options: Just under 6 % Cu
Approx. 33 % Cu
Approx. 54 % Cu
Approx. 1 % Cu

al-cu-havstang-andel-theta.front: An Al–3 % Cu alloy has cooled slowly to room temperature. Approximately what weight fraction of $\theta$ (CuAl₂) does it have? ($\alpha$ then has almost 0 % Cu and $\theta$ approx. 54 % Cu.)
al-cu-havstang-andel-theta.back:
![The Al corner of the Al–Cu phase diagram with the aluminium phase (Al), the eutectic line at 548 °C and the phase θ = CuAl₂](/kort/materialteknik/al-cu-alhornet.svg)

The lever rule between $\alpha$ (≈ 0 % Cu) and $\theta$ (≈ 54 % Cu): fraction of $\theta$ $= \dfrac{3-0}{54-0} \approx 0.056$, i.e. approx. 6 %, and approx. 94 % $\alpha$. 3 % is the Cu content of the alloy, not the fraction of $\theta$; since $\theta$ itself consists of just over half Cu, the fraction of $\theta$ becomes almost twice as large as the Cu content. Approx. 9 % is obtained if one calculates against the eutectic composition (approx. 33 % Cu) instead of against $\theta$.
options: Approx. 6 %
Approx. 9 %
Approx. 94 %

vad-beror-ett-materials-densitet-pa-for.front: What factors does the density of a material depend on?
vad-beror-ett-materials-densitet-pa-for.back:
* The atomic weight of the atoms in the material
* The number of atoms/volume
* The density of composites depends on the volume fraction and density of the constituent materials
* The density of polymer foams, wood etc. is low because of the voids.

atombindningar-kan-jamforas-med-linjara.front: Atomic bonds can be compared with linear springs. Why is this, and why is it done?
atombindningar-kan-jamforas-med-linjara.back:
Atomic bonds are usually likened to linear springs because they have similar properties.
If:
S = the stiffness of the atomic bond
n = the number of bonds/area
We get:
Young's modulus = S x n

* Elastic behaviour = the material behaves
like a spring, springs back on
unloading
* A deep bond energy curve gives:
  - High Young's modulus
  - High melting temperature

vad-har-ett-materials-atombindningar.front: What influence do a material's atomic bonds have on its properties?
vad-har-ett-materials-atombindningar.back:
* Affect stiffness, thermal expansion,
melting temperature, electrical conductivity etc.
* Cannot be changed by processing

hur-ser-ett-typiskt-dragprov-ut-for-ett.front: What does a typical tensile test look like for a brittle material?
hur-ser-ett-typiskt-dragprov-ut-for-ett.back:
* Elastic behaviour up to
the ultimate tensile strength
* Ultimate tensile strength = the stress
at which fracture occurs
* Ceramics, glass

hur-ser-ett-typiskt-dragprov-ut-for-ett-.front: What does a typical tensile test look like for a ductile material?
hur-ser-ett-typiskt-dragprov-ut-for-ett-.back:
* Elastic behaviour up to
the yield strength
* Yield strength = the stress at which
the material starts to yield
* Ultimate tensile strength = the highest stress
* Elastic unloading even in the plastic
region
* Metals, semicrystalline thermoplastics (between Tg and Tm)

vilka-egenskaper-kan-observeras.front: Which properties can be observed/determined by means of a tensile test?
vilka-egenskaper-kan-observeras.back:
![Stress–strain curve from a tensile test with E, Rp0.2, Rm and elongation at break](/kort/materialteknik/dragprovkurva.svg)

* Young's modulus (stiffness) GPa
* Yield strength (starts to yield) MPa
* Ultimate tensile strength (highest stress before fracture) MPa
* Elongation at break (plastic strain after fracture) %
* The area under the curve: the work of fracture, i.e. the energy per unit volume up to fracture. (Toughness in the sense of resistance to crack growth, fracture toughness, however, cannot be measured with a tensile test, since the specimen has no crack.)

dragprov-rp02-bestamning.front: How is the yield strength $R_{p0.2}$ determined from a tensile test curve?
dragprov-rp02-bestamning.back:
![Stress–strain curve from a tensile test with E, Rp0.2, Rm and elongation at break](/kort/materialteknik/dragprovkurva.svg)

The yield strength is determined with a standardised offset method: $R_{p0.2}$ is the stress at 0.2 % permanent (plastic) strain. The highest stress of the curve is the ultimate tensile strength $R_m$ (the tensile strength), and the slope in the elastic region is Young's modulus, $E = \Delta\sigma/\Delta\varepsilon$.
options: A line is drawn parallel to the elastic part of the curve, offset by 0.2 % strain, and the yield strength is the stress where the line intersects the curve.
It is the highest stress of the curve.
It is the stress when the specimen breaks.
It is the slope of the elastic part of the curve.

dragprov-rm-vid-brott.front: The ultimate tensile strength $R_m$ is the stress at the moment the test specimen breaks in a tensile test of a ductile metal.
dragprov-rm-vid-brott.back:
![Stress–strain curve from a tensile test with E, Rp0.2, Rm and elongation at break](/kort/materialteknik/dragprovkurva.svg)

False. The ultimate tensile strength (tensile strength) $R_m$ is the highest stress of the curve. For a ductile metal the engineering stress falls after the maximum, when the specimen necks, so the stress at fracture is lower than $R_m$.
options: True
False

styvheten-hos-kompositer-beror-pa-fler.front: The stiffness of composites depends on more factors than that of homogeneous materials; name at least two of these.
