ttt-avbruten-perlitomvandling.back: The TTT diagram shows how long it takes for unstable austenite to transform into pearlite at different temperatures. When the hold is interrupted, three quarters remain as austenite. On quenching the carbon does not have time to diffuse, so the remaining austenite becomes martensite. Pearlite that has already formed does not become martensite, since only austenite can transform into martensite. Ferrite with spheroidised cementite is obtained by soft annealing.
options: Approx. 25 % pearlite and 75 % martensite
100 % pearlite, since the transformation continues during quenching
100 % martensite, since the pearlite transforms during quenching
Ferrite with spheroidised cementite

mjukglodgat-normaliserat-jamforelse.front: Two samples of the same eutectoid steel have been heat treated differently: one has been soft annealed and the other normalised. Which statements are correct?
mjukglodgat-normaliserat-jamforelse.back: Both treatments give the equilibrium phases ferrite and cementite, and at the same carbon content the lever rule gives the same phase fractions. What differs is the shape of the cementite: normalising (austenitising and slow cooling) gives lamellar pearlite, while soft annealing (heating below approx. 723 °C) through diffusion gives spheroidised cementite, a lower yield strength and a steel that is easier to machine.
options: In the soft-annealed sample the cementite is spheroidised, as round particles in ferrite.
The normalised sample has lamellar pearlite, alternating lamellae of ferrite and cementite.
Both samples have the same fractions of ferrite and cementite.
The soft-annealed sample has a higher fraction of ferrite, since the cementite has dissolved.

stal-varmebehandling-strackgrans-ordning.front: The same medium-carbon steel is heat treated in three ways: soft annealing, normalising, and hardening followed by tempering. Which order applies to the yield strength, from lowest to highest?
stal-varmebehandling-strackgrans-ordning.back: Soft annealing gives spheroidised cementite and a lower yield strength, so that the steel becomes easy to machine. Normalising gives the equilibrium structure with lamellar pearlite. Hardening and tempering give ferrite with very small cementite particles and are used when hardness and yield strength are important; the fine carbides give the high yield strength. The ductility generally goes the other way, since stronger materials tend to have lower ductility.
options: Soft annealed < normalised < hardened and tempered
Normalised < soft annealed < hardened and tempered
Hardened and tempered < normalised < soft annealed
All three get the same yield strength, since the carbon content is the same

vad-kannetecknar-aluminium.back:
* Lower weight than steel, the density is 2.7 kg/dm3
* FCC structure → good plastic formability
* Good machinability
* Good electrical and thermal conductivity
* Corrosion protection: Al reacts with O₂ and forms a
protective oxide layer on the surface

vad-kannetecknar-magnesium.back:
* Low density 1.8 kg/dm3
* HCP structure → limited plastic formability
* Good machinability
* Good castability, most of it is used as castings
* Forms a porous oxide layer, poorer corrosion protection
* Flammable – but only as powder or thin sheet
* Energy-intensive production

vad-kannetecknar-titan.back:
* Medium density 4.1 kg/dm3
* Excellent strength
* Excellent corrosion protection
* Expensive because of the manufacturing process
* Used in pure form or alloyed
* Biocompatible (not harmful to the body), used e.g. in implants

vad-kannetecknar-koppar-och-dess.front: What characterises Copper and its alloys?
vad-kannetecknar-koppar-och-dess.back:
* High density 8.9 kg/dm3
* Copper: Excellent formability, high electrical and thermal
conductivity, price=50 SEK/kg
* Brass: alloyed with 5-40 % Zn, good formability and machinability.
* Bronze: alloyed with 5-25 % Sn, good strength but little
ductility, often cast
* Bearing bronze has good tribological properties

vad-kannetecknar-nickel-och-sa-kallade.front: What characterises Nickel alloys and so-called superalloys?
vad-kannetecknar-nickel-och-sa-kallade.back:
* Medium density 7.9-8.7 kg/dm3
* Young's modulus: 200-220 GPa
* Yield strength: 272-900 MPa
* Fracture toughness: 127-251 $\text{MPa}\sqrt{\text{m}}$
* Service temperature: -273-1040 °C
* Carbon footprint: 13 kg/kg
* Price: 150 SEK/kg (for superalloys)
* Exceptional high-temperature properties with good
oxidation and corrosion properties
* Alloyed with Cr, Co, Al, Ti Mo,
Zr, Fe, Hf

varfor-anvander-man-inte-alltid-stal.front: Why is steel not always used, given that it is the cheapest?
varfor-anvander-man-inte-alltid-stal.back:
Steel has good mechanical properties, a low environmental impact per kilo and is available in many different variants for different applications at the lowest price, but aluminium has a lower density, still a good price, is easy to work and has good natural corrosion protection.

Steel is good, but in certain situations other materials are chosen because their special properties make them particularly advantageous.

aldring.back:
The last step in precipitation hardening, e.g. of heat-treatable aluminium alloys:

1. Solution treatment: the alloying element is dissolved so that the alloy becomes a single phase ($\alpha$).
2. Quenching: a metastable, supersaturated $\alpha$ phase forms.
3. Ageing: at elevated temperature (artificial ageing) or room temperature (natural ageing), diffusion gives small, uniformly distributed precipitates, which raise the yield strength.

The size of the precipitates depends on time and temperature, which gives the underaged, peak-aged (highest yield strength) and overaged conditions.

superlegering.back: Usually Ni-based alloys that have excellent high-temperature properties, oxidation and corrosion resistance.

quiz-magnesium-2-ratt.back: Magnesium has an HCP structure with few slip systems, which gives limited plastic formability. It has good castability and good machinability, and about 75 % is used as castings. Magnesium is relatively brittle: the fracture toughness of Mg alloys is 12 to 18 $\text{MPa}\sqrt{\text{m}}$, lower than that of aluminium alloys (19 to 41 $\text{MPa}\sqrt{\text{m}}$).
options: It has many slip systems for dislocation motion and therefore has a low yield strength.
It is best suited for casting.
It is difficult to machine.
One of the greatest drawbacks is low fracture toughness.

quiz-aluminium-2-ratt.back:
Aluminium reacts with oxygen and forms a protective oxide layer on the surface. Producing aluminium requires considerably more energy per kilo than steel (in the lecture's example with beverage cans 200 versus 23 per kg), but remelting during recycling requires much less energy. Al-Cu alloys can be precipitation hardened. Aluminium has an FCC structure and good plastic formability; it is magnesium that has an HCP structure.

The fourth option of the quiz was an invented alloy name and has been replaced, and "does not corrode" has been made more precise.
options: It is protected against corrosion by an oxide layer (Al₂O₃) that forms on the surface.
It requires less energy per kilo to produce than steel.
It can be precipitation hardened if it is alloyed with copper.
It has an HCP structure and therefore limited plastic formability.

quiz-indelning-och-legering-av-aluminium.front: Classification and alloying of aluminium: which statements are true?
quiz-indelning-och-legering-av-aluminium.back:
On quenching a heat-treatable aluminium alloy, a metastable $\alpha$ phase forms; martensite forms in steel. Solid-solution and precipitation hardening require alloying, so pure aluminium is hardened by strain hardening (e.g. household foil; rolled pure Al has a higher yield strength than annealed). Casting alloys are alloyed with Si to obtain a eutectic, which gives strength and wear resistance and is easy to cast. Aluminium has good machinability.

The quiz wording "The only way to raise the yield strength of pure aluminium is to strain harden" has been softened, since a finer-grained structure also gives a stronger material.
options: When aluminium is quenched, metastable martensite can form.
Pure aluminium is in practice hardened by strain hardening, e.g. rolling.
Casting alloys are alloyed with Si to increase the service temperature.
An advantage of aluminium is that it is easy to machine.

al-varmebehandlingsbara-legeringar.front: Which wrought aluminium alloys are heat-treatable, i.e. can be precipitation hardened?
al-varmebehandlingsbara-legeringar.back: Aluminium alloys are divided into wrought alloys and casting alloys. Of the wrought alloys, 2xxx, 6xxx and 7xxx are heat-treatable: they are precipitation hardened and get a high yield strength (e.g. the 2000 and 7000 series in aerospace). The 1000, 3000 and 5000 series are not heat-treatable, i.e. cannot be precipitation hardened, and are instead hardened by solid-solution and strain hardening.
options: The 2xxx, 6xxx and 7xxx series
The 3xxx and 5xxx series
The 1000 series (foil, electrical conductors)
All wrought alloys, regardless of alloying element

al-toppaldrat.front: In ageing of a heat-treatable aluminium alloy: which condition gives the highest yield strength?
al-toppaldrat.back: Peak-aged material is as strong as the alloy can become, with moderate toughness (e.g. boat masts and slalom poles). Underaged is tougher but has a slightly lower yield strength. Overaged is slightly weaker and tougher but more tolerant of high temperature, since the precipitates have finished growing; it is used e.g. in engine blocks. It is the ageing, which gives small uniformly distributed precipitates, that raises the yield strength after quenching.
options: Underaged
Peak-aged (peak aged, T6)
Overaged
Directly after quenching, before ageing

titan-anvandningstemperatur.front: Titanium alloys can be used at considerably higher temperatures than aluminium and magnesium alloys.
titan-anvandningstemperatur.back: True. According to the lecture's data, titanium alloys can be used up to just under 500 °C (487 °C), compared with approx. 150–200 °C for the aluminium alloys and approx. 190 °C for the magnesium alloys. Among the applications of titanium alloys, the lecture mentions the compressor in jet engines, even though titanium is expensive.
options: True
False

metaller-tillampningar-ti-mg-cu.front: Which pairs of metal and typical application are correct according to the course?
metaller-tillampningar-ti-mg-cu.back: Titanium has excellent strength and corrosion protection and is biocompatible, but is expensive because of the manufacturing process. Magnesium has a low density (1.8 kg/dm³) and good castability; approx. 75 % is used as castings, among other things in aerospace, vehicles, sport and housings, but the service temperature only goes up to approx. 190 °C. Copper has a high density (8.9 kg/dm³) and is chosen for its excellent formability and high electrical and thermal conductivity.
options: Titanium alloys: chemical industry, heat exchangers, implants and the compressor in jet engines
Magnesium alloys: cast housings for cameras, computers and mobile phones
Magnesium alloys: components that are to operate at 500 °C
Copper: lightweight load-bearing structures where low density is most important

magnesium-egenskaper-begransningar.front: Which statements about magnesium alloys are correct?
magnesium-egenskaper-begransningar.back: Magnesium has a low density (1.8 kg/dm³), good castability and good machinability. The HCP structure gives limited plastic formability, so approx. 75 % is used as castings and 25 % as wrought products. The alloys have a low Young's modulus, fracture toughness 12–18 MPa√m and a service temperature up to approx. 190 °C. Typical applications are lightweight cast parts, e.g. housings for machines, cameras, computers and mobile phones.
options: Their Young's modulus (approx. 42–47 GPa) is lower than that of aluminium alloys (approx. 68–76 GPa).
They are used only up to moderate temperatures, about 190 °C.
The HCP structure gives them very good plastic formability.
They are used mostly as wrought products.

al-cu-utskiljningshardning-steg.front: Precipitation hardening of an Al–4 % Cu alloy is done in three steps. What does the solution treatment, the quenching and the ageing each achieve?
al-cu-utskiljningshardning-steg.back:
![The Al corner of the Al–Cu phase diagram with the aluminium phase (Al), eutectic line at 548 °C and the phase θ = CuAl₂](/kort/materialteknik/al-cu-alhornet.svg)

1. **The solution treatment** dissolves all the Cu in the aluminium, so that only $\alpha$ remains. The alloy is heated into the single-phase region $\alpha$: above the solvus line (approx. 500 °C for 4 % Cu) but below the solidus, so that nothing melts. In the course's example it is done just below the eutectic temperature 548 °C.
2. **The quenching** to room temperature keeps all the Cu in solution: the Cu does not have time to diffuse and form $\theta$, so a metastable, supersaturated $\alpha$ phase forms. On slow cooling, $\theta$ would instead form as coarse particles, mainly in the grain boundaries.
3. **The ageing** at moderately elevated temperature (or at room temperature, natural ageing) lets the Cu diffuse short distances, so that small, uniformly distributed $\theta$ precipitates form in $\alpha$. They obstruct dislocation motion and raise the yield strength. Time and temperature determine the size of the precipitates: underaged, peak-aged or overaged.

vad-i-materialtillverkningsprocessen.front: What in the materials production process requires energy, and what does this mean for the environment?
vad-i-materialtillverkningsprocessen.back:
Energy-intensive processes:

* Energy for reduction of mineral to metal
* Other energy for manufacturing and forming, transport, use. Can be reduced by reusing heat.

Environmental impact:

* Intrusion into nature
* Emissions of CO₂
* Other emissions and pollutants
* CO₂ is used as a measure of environmental impact (carbon footprint)

hur-ateranvandningsbara-ar-egentligen.front: How recyclable are metals really? What challenges are there?
hur-ateranvandningsbara-ar-egentligen.back:
* Metal scrap is an excellent raw material for metal production
* Requires less energy than production from ore
* Gives a lower environmental impact
* Metal produced from scrap can give as good a material as metal produced from mineral

Challenges:

* The alloy content must be controlled – problems with mixed scrap and metal impurities
* Copper and tin ruin steel
* Fe embrittles Al
* Lead, cadmium and mercury are often undesirable in
alloys
* The scrap must be collected, transported, sorted

hur-bra-ar-aluminium-sett-ur-ett.front: How good is aluminium from a sustainability perspective?
hur-bra-ar-aluminium-sett-ur-ett.back:
Aluminium:

* Al is one of the elements that are in good supply
* Production of primary aluminium requires a lot of energy, considerably more per kilo than steel
* Remelting during recycling requires much less energy, partly because the melting temperature is lower than that of steel → suitable for products that can be recycled, less suitable for products that cannot be recycled

Problems in recycling aluminium:

* The alloy content must lie within the tolerances for the alloy, so scrap of different alloys must be sorted and kept separate.

hur-bra-ar-stal-respektive-rostfritt.front: How good are steel and stainless steel, respectively, from a sustainability perspective?
hur-bra-ar-stal-respektive-rostfritt.back:
Steel:

* Good supply in the Earth's crust
* Relatively low environmental impact per kg
* High strength in relation to environmental impact
* Corrodes, often requires surface treatment
* High-strength steels can be used in lightweight structures

Stainless steel:

* Alloy of iron, Cr (approx. 18 %), Ni (approx. 8 %), possibly Mo (2 %)
* The supply of the alloying elements in the Earth's crust is comparatively small
* The alloying elements can be unhealthy and allergenic in free form.
Usually not bound in stainless steel.
* Good corrosion resistance and service life. Should be recycled.

vad-finns-det-for-problem-med.front: What problems are there with recycling mixed scrap?
vad-finns-det-for-problem-med.back:
* When reusing scrap, control of the alloying elements is a problem
* Surplus alloying elements and contaminating metals may be or are uneconomical to remove
* Sorted scrap is more useful and has a higher value

vad-ar-co-footprint-respektive-embodied.front: What are the "CO₂ footprint" and the "Embodied Energy", respectively?
vad-ar-co-footprint-respektive-embodied.back:
CO₂ footprint:

* Amount of CO₂ formed in the production of 1 kg of material

For metals:
- CO₂ is formed in the production of energy
- CO₂ is formed in chemical reactions during the reduction of ore to metal

Embodied energy:

* The energy required to produce 1 kg of the material

For metals:
- Energy required for the reduction reaction
- Transport, heating, processes

hur-ser-tillgangen-pa-metaller-i.front: What is the supply of metals in the Earth's crust like?
hur-ser-tillgangen-pa-metaller-i.back:
* The most common metals are present in large quantities in the Earth's crust: Fe, Al, Mg, Ti
* Some alloying elements are present in limited quantities in the Earth's crust
* 69 elements are considered strategic or critical: rare
earth metals, the platinum group, fissile elements (U, Th, Pu), W, Ta, Nb, Ga, In

sammanfatta-lite-kort-hur-metaller.front: Summarise briefly how well suited metals are for recycling.
sammanfatta-lite-kort-hur-metaller.back:
* Metals are well suited for recycling
  - Saves resources and energy
  - Can give as good a material
* Problems with impurities and alloying elements
* CO₂ footprint and embodied energy give some
guidance – can be used in material indices
* Should look at the total environmental impact over the
life cycle

quiz-miljoegenskaper-vad-ar-sant-tva-rat.front: Environmental properties: which statements are true?
quiz-miljoegenskaper-vad-ar-sant-tva-rat.back: The CO₂ footprint and embodied energy can be used in material indices, by replacing the density $\rho$ with $CO_2\,\rho$ or $H_m\,\rho$ when emissions or energy are to be minimised. Recycling reduces the need for raw material, the energy consumption and the CO₂ emissions. The course's "materials for tomorrow" should have both a low CO₂ footprint and a low embodied energy. Steel has low CO₂ emissions per kilo; it is the large usage that gives large global emissions.
options: The CO₂ footprint and embodied energy can provide guidance in materials selection.
Materials with a high CO₂ footprint should be recycled.
Environmentally smart materials have a low CO₂ footprint and a high embodied energy.
The problem with steel is the large CO₂ emissions per kilo of steel produced.

hallb-eco-audit-vagracken.front: In the course's eco audit example with crash barriers: which life-cycle phase dominates for a static roadside barrier and for a barrier mounted on a car, respectively?
hallb-eco-audit-vagracken.back: An eco audit shows in which life-cycle phase most resources are used, and thereby what the materials selection should optimise. For the static roadside barrier, material production dominates, so the criterion becomes bending strength per unit energy, index $\sigma_y^{2/3}/(H_p\,\rho)$. For the barrier on the car, use dominates, so the criterion becomes bending strength per unit mass, $\sigma_y^{2/3}/\rho$.
options: The roadside barrier: material production. The car's barrier: use.
The roadside barrier: use. The car's barrier: material production.
Material production in both cases.
Use in both cases.

hallb-co2-i-materialindex.front: How is the CO₂ footprint taken into account in a material index for a light, strong beam, $\sigma_y^{2/3}/\rho$?
hallb-co2-i-materialindex.back: To minimise CO₂ emissions or embodied energy instead of mass, $\rho$ is replaced by $CO_2\,\rho$ or $H_m\,\rho$ respectively, where $CO_2$ and $H_m$ are the emissions and the energy, respectively, per kg of material. The index then becomes $\sigma_y^{2/3}/(CO_2\,\rho)$, and in the course's crash barrier example $\sigma_y^{2/3}/(H_p\,\rho)$ is used in the same way. Multiplying the index by the CO₂ footprint would favour materials with high emissions.
options: The density $\rho$ is replaced by $CO_2\,\rho$ (CO₂ footprint per kg times density)
The index is multiplied by the CO₂ footprint
The yield strength $\sigma_y$ is replaced by the CO₂ footprint
The CO₂ footprint cannot be used in a material index, it requires a life cycle assessment

hallb-hoghallfast-mindre-material.front: High-strength metals can reduce the environmental impact of a product, since less material is needed.
hallb-hoghallfast-mindre-material.back: True. The lecture mentions high-strength metals, which give less material, together with better design, improved manufacturing methods, light metals and composites when low weight is needed, and recycled metal as ways of designing more environmentally friendly with metals.
options: True
False

plast-bionedbrytbar-biobaserad.back:
**Biodegradable:** the plastic is broken down by microorganisms into, among other things, carbon dioxide, water and new biomass (without oxygen also methane). To count as fully biodegradable according to the European standard EN 13432, at least 90 % must have been broken down in less than 6 months.

**Bio-based:** the plastic is made from biomass, i.e. renewable raw materials from plants, animals or microorganisms, instead of fossil (petrochemical) raw materials.

The two properties are independent of each other: the raw material does not determine whether the plastic is biodegradable.

plast-bio-indelning-exempel.front: Which examples are correctly placed in the classification by raw material (bio-based or fossil) and biodegradability?
plast-bio-indelning-exempel.back: The course's four-quadrant diagram has the raw material on one axis and the biodegradability on the other. PLA and starch blends are both bio-based and biodegradable. Bio-based PE, PET and PA are made from renewable raw materials but are not biologically degraded; bio-based PE has the same repeating unit as fossil PE, what differs is the raw material. PCL and PBAT are fossil-based but biodegradable. Conventional plastics such as PE, PP and PET are fossil-based and not biodegradable.
options: PLA: bio-based and biodegradable
Bio-based PE: bio-based but not biodegradable, with the same chemical structure as ordinary PE
PCL: fossil-based but biodegradable
Conventional PP: fossil-based and biodegradable

hallb-atervinning-ensam-racker-inte.front: Which statements about recycling of metals are correct according to the course?
hallb-atervinning-ensam-racker-inte.back: A circular economy model does not work on its own, since demand on the market currently exceeds the amount of scrap, according to the lecture by about two thirds. Therefore all stages of metal use need to be improved, from primary production and manufacturing to use and recycling. Metals are well suited for recycling, save resources and energy and can give as good a material. For many critical metals, e.g. gallium, indium and germanium in semiconductors, the recycling rate is on the other hand very low.
options: The demand for metals is today greater than the amount of scrap available for recycling.
All materials can be recycled, but the recycling costs energy and resources.
Metals always lose their properties when they are recycled.
Critical metals such as gallium and indium are already recycled to a very high degree.

hallbara-produkter-kombination.front: According to the course there are no sustainable materials. How can a product nevertheless be made more sustainable?
hallbara-produkter-kombination.back: Through a combination of the right materials selection, good design, the right manufacturing method and the right recycling, i.e. good engineering. In the materials selection one includes resource consumption, energy consumption and CO₂ emissions over the whole chain (material production, product manufacture, use, disposal and recycling), e.g. with material indices for CO₂ footprint and embodied energy, and chooses recyclable materials. In addition: remanufacturing, reuse and recycling, and valuable products with a long service life.

namn-minst-tva-olika-typer-av-polymerer.front: Name at least two different types of polymers and what characterizes them.
namn-minst-tva-olika-typer-av-polymerer.back:
* Thermoplastics
  - Long polymer chains
  - Weak forces between
the chains
  - Can be shaped with heat
  - Recyclable
* Thermosets
  - Network of molecules
  - Covalent bonds
  - Cannot be shaped with heat
  - Not recyclable
* Rubbers (elastomers)
  - Weakly crosslinked
polymer chains
  - Cannot be shaped with heat
  - Not recyclable

quiz-a-semi-crystalline-polymer-en.front: What is true about a semi-crystalline polymer?
quiz-a-semi-crystalline-polymer-en.back: Thermoplastics are divided into amorphous and semi-crystalline. Above Tm the polymer is a melt, and in the molten state all polymers are amorphous. Whether a polymer can become semi-crystalline depends on how ordered the chain is (the chains must be able to pack side by side), not on casting; an amorphous polymer does not become semi-crystalline by being cast. Tm lies above Tg: at Tg the amorphous parts soften while the crystals hold the material together all the way up to Tm.
options: It is a type of thermoplastic
It is amorphous above the melting temperature
It is manufactured by casting an amorphous polymer (e.g. PS)
It melts below the glass transition temperature

quiz-thermoplastic-polymers-termoplastis.back: Thermoplastics are either amorphous or semi-crystalline. As melts they are shear thinning: the viscosity decreases as the shear rate increases. They do not harden on heating; the modulus drops sharply at Tg (and at Tm for semi-crystalline ones). Polymers are thermal insulators because long molecules can distribute the thermal energy over many vibration modes.
options: As melts they have a shear thinning viscosity function
They are amorphous or semi-crystalline
They harden when the temperature increases
They are thermally conductive polymers

quiz-copolymers-sampolymerer-tva-ratta-s.back: A copolymer has two or more monomer types in the same chain and can be linear or (long-chain) branched. Depending on how the monomers are arranged, one distinguishes random, alternating, block and graft copolymers; impact resistant polystyrene (PS-HI), for example, is made by grafting polystyrene onto polybutadiene. The polydispersity index, PDI = Mw/Mn, describes how broad the molecular weight distribution is and has nothing to do with the number of monomer types. Since Mw ≥ Mn, PDI can never be negative.
options: They contain two or more types of monomers in the same chain
They can be linear or branched
They are polymers with a high polydispersity index
They are polymers with a negative polydispersity index

quiz-thermosets-hardplaster-tva-ratta-sv.back: Thermosets are highly crosslinked amorphous polymers. The network is formed during curing from monomers that can bind to more than two other monomers. As amorphous polymers they have a Tg, but they degrade before they can melt and therefore have no Tm. Thermoset is a classification by structure (high degree of crosslinking), not by field of application; epoxy, the most common thermoset, for example has a Tg around 120 °C.
options: They are made from monomers with more than two binding sites (functionality > 2)
They are amorphous
They have no glass transition temperature but have a melting temperature
They are defined as the group of polymers developed for high temperature applications

polymer-mn-mw-berakning.front: A polymer consists of equal numbers of chains with molecular weights 100 000, 200 000 and 300 000 g/mol. What are Mn and Mw?
polymer-mn-mw-berakning.back:
With $n_i$ chains of molecular weight $M_i$ (here $n_i$ equal for all three):

$M_n = \dfrac{\sum n_i M_i}{\sum n_i} = \dfrac{100\,000 + 200\,000 + 300\,000}{3} = 200\,000$ g/mol

$M_w = \dfrac{\sum n_i M_i^2}{\sum n_i M_i} = \dfrac{(1 + 4 + 9)\cdot 10^{10}}{6 \cdot 10^{5}} \approx 233\,333$ g/mol

Mw weights the heavy chains more heavily and therefore becomes larger than Mn; Mw = Mn only holds if all chains are equally long. PDI here becomes approximately $1.17$.
options: Mn = 200 000 g/mol and Mw ≈ 233 000 g/mol
Mn ≈ 233 000 g/mol and Mw = 200 000 g/mol
Mn = Mw = 200 000 g/mol
Mn = 200 000 g/mol and Mw = 300 000 g/mol

polymer-polymerisationsgrad-pe-berakning.front: Estimate the degree of polymerization of a polyethylene with molecular weight 150 000 g/mol (the ethylene monomer weighs 28 g/mol).
polymer-polymerisationsgrad-pe-berakning.back: The degree of polymerization is the number of repeating units: $DP = M/M_0 = 150\,000/28 \approx 5\,357$. The ethylene monomer C₂H₄ weighs $2\cdot 12 + 4\cdot 1 = 28$ g/mol. 3 570 is the answer for a chain of 100 000 g/mol, 10 700 is obtained if one calculates with CH₂ (14 g/mol) instead of the whole monomer, and 4 200 000 is obtained if one multiplies instead of dividing.
options: About 5 360 repeating units
About 3 570 repeating units
About 10 700 repeating units
About 4 200 000 repeating units

polymer-kedjelangd-pe-berakning.front: How long is a fully extended polyethylene molecule with molecular weight 84 000 g/mol? (Repeating unit 28 g/mol, 0.252 nm per unit.)
polymer-kedjelangd-pe-berakning.back: The number of repeating units is $n = 84\,000/28 = 3\,000$. The extended length becomes $l = 3\,000 \cdot 0.252 \text{ nm} = 756 \text{ nm} \approx 0.76$ µm. 0.76 nm is a unit error (nm instead of µm), 1.5 µm is obtained if one uses CH₂ (14 g/mol) as the unit but keeps 0.252 nm, and 21 µm is obtained if one multiplies the molecular weight directly by 0.252 nm instead of the number of units.
options: About 760 nm (0.76 µm)
About 0.76 nm
About 1.5 µm
About 21 µm

polymer-vinylpolymerer-sidogrupper.front: Vinyl polymers have the repeating unit –[CH₂–CHX]ₙ–. Which pairs of side group X and polymer are correct?
polymer-vinylpolymerer-sidogrupper.back: The side groups in the course: X = H gives PE, X = CH₃ gives PP, X = C₆H₅ (phenyl group) gives PS and X = Cl gives PVC. The two incorrect options have swapped PP and PS.
options: X = H gives polyethylene (PE)
X = Cl gives polyvinylchloride (PVC)
X = CH₃ gives polystyrene (PS)
X = C₆H₅ gives polypropylene (PP)

polymer-overgangstemperaturer-per-typ.front: Which transition temperatures do the different types of polymers have?
polymer-overgangstemperaturer-per-typ.back: Amorphous thermoplastics have only Tg. Semi-crystalline ones have Tg, where the amorphous parts soften, and Tm, where the crystals melt. Crosslinked polymers (thermosets and elastomers) are amorphous and therefore have a Tg, but they degrade before they melt and have no Tm.
options: Amorphous thermoplastic: Tg but no Tm
Semi-crystalline thermoplastic: both Tg and Tm
Thermoset: both Tg and Tm
Crosslinked elastomer: Tm but no Tg

polymer-anvandningsintervall-delkristall.front: Within which temperature range is a semi-crystalline thermoplastic used?
polymer-anvandningsintervall-delkristall.back: Between Tg and Tm the amorphous parts have softened while the crystals hold the material together, and the toughness increases in that range. Below Tg semi-crystalline polymers typically become extremely brittle, and above Tm they are melts. The useful range is therefore Tg < T < Tm.
options: Between Tg and Tm
Below Tg
Above Tm
Between Tm and the degradation temperature

polymer-skjuvmodul-amorf-vid-tg.front: What happens to the shear modulus of an amorphous thermoplastic, e.g. PS, when the temperature passes Tg?
polymer-skjuvmodul-amorf-vid-tg.back: At Tg the chains vibrate so strongly that they can move considerably more freely, and the shear modulus drops by about three decades (logarithmic axis in the DMTA curve). An amorphous thermoplastic has no Tm and no crystals; it is in a semi-crystalline polymer that the crystals hold the material together above Tg.
options: It decreases by about three decades (approx. 1 000 times)
It increases, because the chains become locked
It is largely unchanged until Tm is reached
It decreases only slightly, because the crystals hold the material together

polymer-tillsats-mjukgorare.front: Which additive reduces the hardness and stiffness of a plastic?
polymer-tillsats-mjukgorare.back: Plasticizers increase the distance between the molecules, which lowers the stiffness and Tg. Stabilizers protect against thermal and chemical degradation (heat, sunlight, oxygen), antistatic agents prevent the plastic from being charged electrostatically and flame retardants reduce the flammability.
options: Plasticizer
Stabilizer
Antistatic agent
Flame retardant

polymer-pdi-ett-monodispers.front: A PDI of 1 means that all chains in the polymer are equally long.
polymer-pdi-ett-monodispers.back: Since Mw ≥ Mn, PDI = Mw/Mn is always at least 1. Mw = Mn, i.e. PDI = 1, only holds if all chains are equally long (monodisperse polymer). Most polymers are polydisperse with PDI > 1.
options: True
False

polymer-ataktisk-pp-kristallinitet.front: Atactic polypropylene reaches a high degree of crystallinity more easily than isotactic polypropylene.
polymer-ataktisk-pp-kristallinitet.back: It is the other way round. In isotactic PP all CH₃ groups are on the same side, so the chains can pack side by side and reach high crystallinity. In atactic PP the side groups are placed randomly, which makes it difficult for the neighboring chains to lock into an ordered position.
options: True
False

polymer-restmonomer-tg.front: Residues of the monomer that remain in the polymer after the polymerization, and that are soluble in the polymer, raise its Tg.
polymer-restmonomer-tg.back: Residues of the monomer that are soluble in the polymer act as a plasticizer and lower Tg. Plasticizers increase the distance between the molecules so that they move more easily.
options: True
False

polymer-amorf-termoplast-under-tg.front: An amorphous thermoplastic is used, with a safety margin, at temperatures below its Tg.
polymer-amorf-termoplast-under-tg.back: Above Tg an amorphous thermoplastic loses its stiffness, since there are no crystals that hold the material together. The service temperature is therefore T < Tg with a safety margin. For semi-crystalline thermoplastics it is instead Tm that sets the upper limit.
options: True
False

polymer-kovalent-och-van-der-waals.front: In polyethylene the backbone is held together by strong covalent C–C bonds, while the chains are bound to each other by weak van der Waals forces.
polymer-kovalent-och-van-der-waals.back: The C–C bonds in the backbone are covalent and strong, while the forces between the chains are van der Waals forces and weak. Therefore the strength of the polymer is in practice determined by the forces between the chains, and longer chains give a stronger material.
options: True
False

polymer-hdpe-ldpe-kristallinitet.front: HDPE has higher crystallinity than LDPE because the long chain branches of LDPE prevent the chains from packing closely.
polymer-hdpe-ldpe-kristallinitet.back: HDPE consists of linear molecules and can reach a crystallinity of up to approx. 75 %. LDPE has long chain branches that prevent the neighboring chains from approaching and locking side by side, which gives lower crystallinity.
options: True
False

polymer-begrepp-monomer.back: The repeating building block of a polymer: a molecule that can bind to identical molecules and form a polymer chain through polymerization. Example: ethylene (C₂H₄, a gas) is the monomer in polyethylene.

polymer-begrepp-polymerisationsgrad.back: The number of repeating units n in a polymer chain. It can be estimated as the molecular weight divided by the molecular weight of the monomer: $DP = M/M_0$.

polymer-begrepp-takticitet.back: How the side groups are placed along the carbon backbone. Isotactic: all on the same side. Syndiotactic: regularly alternating. Atactic: random. The tacticity determines how high a crystallinity the polymer can reach; isotactic PP becomes more crystalline than atactic.

polymer-begrepp-sampolymer.back: A polymer whose chains contain two or more types of monomers (a homopolymer has only one). Types: random, alternating, block and graft. Examples: ABS (acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene) and SBR (styrene-butadiene-rubber).

polymer-begrepp-polymerblandning.back: A mixture of two or more polymers made to improve the properties of the individual polymers. Unlike in a copolymer, the different monomers do not sit in the same chain. Examples: PP-PC, PVC-ABS and LDPE + HDPE.

polymer-begrepp-sfarulit.back: The largest structure (lengthscale) in a semi-crystalline polymer: the crystals form lamellae, which in turn build up spherulites, and between them there are amorphous regions. Spherulites can be roughly 1 to 500 µm in size, i.e. much larger than the wavelength of visible light, and are clearly visible with polarized light microscopy.

polymer-begrepp-tvarbindning.back: Bonding points, in engineering polymers mostly covalent, that tie the chains together into a network. They are formed during curing from monomers with more than two binding sites. Covalently crosslinked polymers cannot be remelted. A high degree of crosslinking gives a rigid thermoset, a low one gives an elastomer.

polymer-begrepp-glasomvandlingstemperatu.back: The temperature at which an amorphous polymer, or the amorphous parts of a semi-crystalline polymer, goes from a glassy state to a rubbery or molten state. The transition is reversible and is not the melting point; the stiffness drops sharply at Tg.

polymer-varfor-termiska-isolatorer.front: Why are polymers good thermal insulators?
polymer-varfor-termiska-isolatorer.back: In metals heat is conducted as waves of lattice vibrations (phonons). A long polymer molecule can be seen as atoms with bonds that are not equal in all directions, so a temperature increase can be distributed over a very large number of vibration modes in the molecule. That is why polymers insulate. Foams insulate best, e.g. styrofoam (PS-foam), because they contain a lot of air.

polymer-transparens-amorf-delkristallin.front: Why are amorphous thermoplastics transparent while semi-crystalline ones are often translucent or opaque?
polymer-transparens-amorf-delkristallin.back:
**Amorphous** thermoplastics (e.g. PS, PC, PMMA) consist of randomly oriented chains without supramolecular structure and are transparent unless they contain pigments or other additives.

**Semi-crystalline** ones (e.g. PE, PP, PA) contain crystals and amorphous regions with different refractive indices, so light is scattered at the boundaries between them. When the crystals and spherulites are about as large as or larger than the wavelength of visible light, the material becomes translucent or opaque.

polymer-begrepp-mn-mw.front: Number-averaged and weight-averaged molecular weight (Mn and Mw)
polymer-begrepp-mn-mw.back:
A polymer consists of chains of different lengths, so the molecular weight is described by a molecular weight distribution and averages:

* **Mn**, number-averaged molecular weight: an ordinary average over the chains, $M_n = \sum n_i M_i / \sum n_i$
* **Mw**, weight-averaged molecular weight: weights the heavy chains more heavily, $M_w = \sum n_i M_i^2 / \sum n_i M_i$

$M_w \ge M_n$, and the polydispersity index $\mathrm{PDI} = M_w/M_n$ is a measure of how broad the distribution is. Two polymers with the same Mn can therefore have distributions of different breadth and different PDI.

polymer-begrepp-langkedjeforgrening.front: Short chain and long chain branching
polymer-begrepp-langkedjeforgrening.back: Branching describes the topology of the polymer molecule. Most engineering polymers are linear, short-chain branched or long-chain branched. With short chain branching the backbone has short side chains, e.g. HDPE (approx. 4–10 per 1 000 C-atoms) and LLDPE (approx. 10–35), and the molecule still counts as linear. With long chain branching, as in LDPE, the chain has long branches. The branches prevent the neighboring chains from packing closely, so HDPE (linear) reaches much higher crystallinity (up to approx. 75 %) than LDPE. Branching is something other than tacticity, which describes how the side groups are placed along the chain.

polymer-topologi-lldpe.front: LLDPE has approx. 10–35 short side chains per 1 000 carbon atoms. How is the molecule classified in the course's classification by topology?
polymer-topologi-lldpe.back: Both HDPE (approx. 4–10 short side chains per 1 000 C) and LLDPE (linear low density polyethylene) count as linear, short-chain branched molecules, while LDPE has long chain branching. Crosslinked polymers have bonds between the chains, so that they form a network.
options: Linear, with short chain branching
Long-chain branched
Crosslinked
None of them, since only completely unbranched chains count as linear

polymer-struktur-bild-hardplast.front: The image shows three schematic polymer structures. Which one shows a crosslinked polymer, such as a thermoset? ![Three schematic polymer structures labeled A, B and C](/kort/materialteknik/polymerstrukturer-abc.svg)
polymer-struktur-bild-hardplast.back: A has chains that are bound together in a network of crosslinks: highly crosslinked gives a thermoset, weakly crosslinked an elastomer. B has chains folded into crystalline lamellae with disordered (amorphous) chains in between: a semi-crystalline thermoplastic, where the lamellae build up spherulites. C is randomly entangled chains without order, "a bowl of spaghetti": an amorphous thermoplastic.
options: A
B
C

polymer-modulkurva-delkristallin.front: A DMTA measurement shows, as the temperature is raised: first a moderate drop in the modulus, then a plateau where the material is still solid, and finally a very steep drop. Which type of polymer is it most likely?
polymer-modulkurva-delkristallin.back: The modulus is plotted on a logarithmic scale. In a semi-crystalline polymer the amorphous parts soften at Tg, but the crystals hold the material, which is still solid, together until they melt at Tm. An amorphous thermoplastic has no Tm: at Tg the modulus drops about three decades and above Tg it flows as a melt. Crosslinked polymers (thermosets and elastomers) have a Tg but degrade before they melt.
options: A semi-crystalline thermoplastic: the drop at Tg in the amorphous parts, the steep drop at Tm
An amorphous thermoplastic: the drop at Tg, the steep drop at Tm
A thermoset: the drop at Tm, the steep drop when the crosslinks melt
An elastomer: the drop at Tm, the steep drop at Tg

polymer-modulkurva-tvarbunden.front: The modulus of a polymer drops at Tg and then levels out at a lower level, which holds until the material degrades at high temperature without melting. What type of polymer is it?
polymer-modulkurva-tvarbunden.back: Crosslinked polymers are amorphous and have a Tg, but they degrade before they can melt, so above Tg they are only weakly softening. Tg depends on the degree of crosslinking: for weakly crosslinked elastomers it can be as low as approx. −50 °C, for thermosets as high as approx. 120 °C (e.g. epoxy). An amorphous thermoplastic flows as a melt above Tg, and a semi-crystalline thermoplastic gets a steep drop at Tm.
options: A crosslinked polymer (elastomer or thermoset)
An amorphous thermoplastic
A semi-crystalline thermoplastic
A polymer melt

polymer-hardplaster-forkortningar.front: Which of the following are thermosets?
polymer-hardplaster-forkortningar.back: In the course book's abbreviation table, MF, PF, UF, UP, PUR (polyurethane) and EP (epoxy) are thermosets (TS). Epoxy is the most common thermoset, and 80 % of thermosets are used as matrix in composites. PMMA and PP are thermoplastics. Thermosets are highly crosslinked and amorphous and cannot be remelted.
options: PF, phenol formaldehyde
EP, epoxy
MF, melamine formaldehyde
UP, unsaturated polyester
PMMA, polymethylmethacrylate
PP, polypropylene

polymer-begrepp-tillsatser.back:
Plastic = polymer + additives. Common additives:

* **Stabilizers:** protect against thermal and chemical degradation (heat, sunlight, air, oxygen)
* **Dyes (pigments):** color the plastic
* **Flame retardants:** reduce the flammability; often relatively large additions, approx. 10 %
* **Antistatic agents:** prevent the plastic from being charged electrostatically; often approx. 1 %
* **Plasticizers:** increase the distance between the molecules and lower hardness, stiffness and Tg

quiz-the-melt-flow-index-smaltflodesinde.front: Which statements about the melt flow index (MFI) are correct?
quiz-the-melt-flow-index-smaltflodesinde.back: MFI is the mass of polymer in grams that a piston loaded with a standardized weight pushes out through a cylindrical die in 10 minutes, at a standardized temperature. The unit is therefore g/10 min. A thicker melt (higher viscosity) gives less extruded material and thus a lower MFI. MFI is a measure of flow, not a measure of strain at break, and it is measured in a melt flow indexer with a piston and a die, not in an extruder.
options: It is given in grams per 10 minutes.
It is inversely proportional to the viscosity: higher viscosity gives a lower MFI.
It measures the strain at break of polymers.
It is determined in experiments with a single screw extruder without a die.

quiz-extrusion-extrudering-tva-ratta-sva.front: Which statements about extrusion are correct?
quiz-extrusion-extrudering-tva-ratta-sva.back: Fiber spinning is a secondary shaping operation coupled to extrusion: the melt is extruded through a die with one or more orifices and drawn by pairs of take-off rolls. The extruder die gives the final profile, e.g. pipes, films, filaments and profiles. Extrusion is a processing method, not a testing method. The pellets should not melt in the hopper: the solids conveying zone is often cooled precisely so that the pellets do not melt and clog the barrel inlet, and melting takes place only in the heated part of the barrel.
options: It is the base process for fiber spinning.
It can be used to manufacture pipes.
It is a method to test the thermal properties of polymers.
It requires the polymer to be melted already in the hopper.

quiz-shear-thinning-skjuvtunning-tva-rat.front: Which statements about shear thinning are correct?
quiz-shear-thinning-skjuvtunning-tva-rat.back:
![Viscosity function of a polymer melt on a log-log plot with a zero-shear plateau, a shear-thinning region and a plateau at high shear rates](/kort/materialteknik/viskositetsfunktion.svg)

The viscosity function has three regions in order of increasing shear rate: the zero-shear viscosity at low shear rates, the shear-thinning region and the infinite-shear viscosity. In the shear-thinning region the chains stretch, orient in the flow direction and disentangle, so the viscosity decreases as the shear rate increases. The first region is thus at low, not high, shear rates. Shear thinning concerns the viscosity of the melt, not toughness.
options: It is caused by the polymer chains gradually orienting in the flow direction, stretching and disentangling.
It is the second region of the viscosity curve of a polymer melt.
It is the first region of the viscosity function, at very high shear rates.
It refers to a reduction in the toughness of polymeric materials.

quiz-during-polymer-processing-vid.front: Which statements about the shear rate during polymer processing are correct?
quiz-during-polymer-processing-vid.back: Small or slow deformations do not change the orientation of the chains, whereas large or fast deformations orient the molecules in the flow direction. Each processing method has its typical shear rate range; fiber spinning gives the most orientation of the chains, whereas compression molding, which takes place at low shear rates, gives little orientation. Since polymer melts are shear thinning, the viscosity depends on the shear rate. The shear rate has the unit 1/s; Pa s is the unit of viscosity.
options: High shear rates give stronger molecular orientation in the flow direction.
The typical shear rates differ between processes such as extrusion, injection molding and fiber spinning.
The shear rate does not affect the viscosity.
The shear rate is measured in pascal-seconds (Pa s).

quiz-die-swelling-formsprutningssvallnin.front: Which statements about die swelling are correct?
quiz-die-swelling-formsprutningssvallnin.back: In the die the melt is subjected to shear flow in the shear-thinning region, so the chains are stretched, oriented and may disentangle. When the melt has left the die and is at atmospheric pressure, the chains relax back towards their preferred conformation, and the extrudate becomes larger than the die opening. It is thus an elastic effect of a viscoelastic fluid; a Newtonian (purely viscous) fluid does not swell. Melt flow is measured with MFI, not with die swelling.
options: It is a viscoelastic effect that occurs when a polymer melt exits the die.
It is caused by the relaxation of oriented and stretched polymer chains.
It is a measure of the melt flow rate.
It occurs only in Newtonian fluids.

quiz-the-viscosity-function-of-a-polymer.front: Which statements about the viscosity function of a polymer melt are correct?
quiz-the-viscosity-function-of-a-polymer.back:
![Viscosity function of a polymer melt on a log-log plot with a zero-shear plateau, a shear-thinning region and a plateau at high shear rates](/kort/materialteknik/viskositetsfunktion.svg)

The viscosity function is plotted as viscosity versus shear rate on a log-log plot. Polymer melts are called shear thinning because the viscosity decreases when they are sheared faster; in the zero-shear region it is constant, and the plateau at very high shear rates is difficult to reach for melts. The curves drop when the temperature is raised, and they differ between polymers (e.g. ABS, PC and PA6) and depend on the molecular weight and the molecular weight distribution.
options: It has three main regions: a zero-shear plateau, a shear-thinning region and an infinite-shear plateau.
It shows that the viscosity overall decreases with increasing shear rate (shear thinning).
It is independent of temperature.
It is the same for all polymer melts.

quiz-the-injection-molding-cycle.front: Which statements about the injection molding cycle are correct?
quiz-the-injection-molding-cycle.back: The cycle starts when the mold closes; then the melt is injected, holding pressure is applied, the next shot is fed forward and the part is ejected once it has cooled. The cycle time is $t_{\text{cycle}} = t_{\text{closing}} + t_{\text{cooling}} + t_{\text{ejection}}$, and the cooling time, during which the part solidifies in the mold, is approximately 80% of it. It is the part in the mold that has to be cooled, not the screw, and the cycle is a manufacturing sequence, not a measurement method.
options: It is dominated by the solidification time.
It starts with the closing of the mold.
It measures the melt viscosity.
It is dominated by the cooling of the screw.

quiz-a-single-screw-extruder-en.front: Which statements about a single screw extruder are correct?
quiz-a-single-screw-extruder-en.back:
![Single screw extruder with hopper, barrel, screw, die and the three zones](/kort/materialteknik/enskruvsextruder.svg)

In the metering zone the pressure is built up that pushes the melt through the die at the end of the extruder; the pressure is highest closest to the die, not at the hopper. The die gives the profile of the product, e.g. pipes and tubular films, and with film casting or film blowing as a secondary shaping operation it becomes thin films. The pellets do not melt in the hopper; the solids conveying zone is often cooled precisely to prevent that.
options: The screw has a metering zone that builds up the pressure during flow.
It can be used to manufacture pipes and thin films.
The pressure is built up in the solids conveying zone at the hopper.
It melts the pellets directly in the hopper.

quiz-injection-molding-machines.front: Which statements about injection molding machines are correct?
quiz-injection-molding-machines.back: An injection molding machine consists of an injection unit, a plasticizing unit, a mold and a clamping unit, and the pellets are fed in through a hopper. The machine operates in a cycle (closing, injection, holding pressure, cooling, ejection), not continuously. Semi-crystalline polymers are also injection molded; the lecture only points out that the heat of crystallization must be removed and that they shrink more, which is partially compensated for by longer packing times and higher pressure.
options: They operate continuously without a cycle.
They have a hopper for feeding pellets.
They have an injection unit and a clamping unit.
They cannot be used for semi-crystalline polymers.

quiz-p-v-t-diagrams-refer-to-p-v-t-diagr.front: What do p-V-T diagrams stand for, and what do they show?
quiz-p-v-t-diagrams-refer-to-p-v-t-diagr.back:
![p-V-T diagram: amorphous polymer with a change in slope at Tg and semi-crystalline polymer with a jump at Tm](/kort/materialteknik/pvt-amorf-delkristallin.svg)

A p-V-T diagram shows the specific volume (volume per mass, i.e. the inverse of the density) as a function of temperature at different pressures. The diagram shows, for example, the change in slope at the glass transition for amorphous polymers, the jump at crystallization for semi-crystalline ones, and that high pressure raises Tg and Tm. Viscosity and MFI are not part of the diagram.
options: Pressure, volume and temperature (pressure-volume-temperature).
They describe the relationship between the density and the temperature of a polymer, also in the melt state.
Pressure, viscosity and temperature.
They quantify the melt flow index.

quiz-extrusion-extrudering.front: Which statements about extrusion as a process are correct?
quiz-extrusion-extrudering.back: The principle of extrusion is that a melt is pumped through a die, and the pressure for this is built up in the metering zone of the screw. With film casting as a secondary shaping operation it becomes thin films, e.g. for packaging. The pellets melt only in the heated part of the barrel, not in the hopper. The closing of the mold is the first step of the injection molding cycle; in extrusion there is no closed mold, instead the melt is pushed out through the die and gives products of in principle continuous length.
options: It relies on pressure being built up in the metering zone so that the polymer is pushed through the die.
It can be used to manufacture thin packaging films.
It requires the pellets to be melted in the hopper.
It starts with the closing of the mold.

quiz-injection-moulding-formsprutning.front: Which statements about injection molding are correct?
quiz-injection-moulding-formsprutning.back: Injection molding is suited for mass-produced parts with complex shapes and is more versatile than extrusion in terms of which products can be manufactured, so it is not limited to constant wall thickness. Flash occurs when the holding pressure is too high: the pressure in the cavity exceeds the clamping force of the machine and melt is forced out at the parting line of the mold. Too low a holding pressure instead gives too much shrinkage.
options: It operates according to the injection molding cycle.
It can only manufacture products with constant wall thickness.
It can lead to flash if the holding pressure is too low.
The machine has an injection unit.

quiz-film-casting-filmcasting.front: Which statements about film casting are correct?
quiz-film-casting-filmcasting.back: In film casting the melt is extruded through a slit die and drawn onto a chill roll, which cools the film and imposes a drawing ratio on it. The result is thin films, e.g. for packaging. Secondary shaping operations (fiber spinning, film casting, film blowing) belong to extrusion, not to injection molding. Die swelling is an elastic effect at the die, not the aim of the process.
options: The purpose is to induce die swelling.
It is a secondary shaping operation after extrusion.
It is a secondary shaping operation after injection molding.
It is used to manufacture thin polymer films.

quiz-the-components-of-a-mold-for-inject.front: Which components are included in a mold for injection molding?
quiz-the-components-of-a-mold-for-inject.back: The mold consists of the sprue and runners, gate, mold cavity, cooling system (sometimes) and ejector system (typically pins). The metering zone belongs to the extruder screw, not to the mold. Shish-kebab is a crystalline structure that can form in the material when it is sheared and cooled simultaneously, not a part of the mold.
options: The metering zone of the screw
Shish-kebab crystalline structures
Ejector pins
In some cases a cooling system

quiz-during-solidification-under-stelnin.front: Which statements about solidification after processing are correct?
quiz-during-solidification-under-stelnin.back: Processing can lock in out-of-equilibrium structures, e.g. flow-induced orientation and stretching of the chains. Rapid cooling lowers the crystallinity because the microstructure is frozen before the chains have had time to organize completely; in this way crystallization can even be prevented (cf. PET bottles). Shish-kebab structures are crystalline structures and form in semi-crystalline polymers (most commonly isotactic PP and PE), not in amorphous ones. On cooling, the polymer solidifies through the glass transition or crystallization; the chains do not degrade.
options: The orientation of the polymer chains can be frozen.
The crystallization can be frozen so that it does not have time to be completed.
Shear flow can result in shish-kebab structures in amorphous polymers.
Polymers always depolymerize on cooling.

reo-viskositet.back: The resistance of a fluid to flow. Newton's law of viscosity: $\sigma = \eta\dot{\gamma}$, i.e. the shear stress $\sigma$ is proportional to the shear rate $\dot{\gamma}$, and the proportionality constant $\eta$ is the (shear) viscosity. The unit is Pa s. For a Newtonian fluid $\eta$ depends only on temperature and pressure; for a polymer melt it also depends on the shear rate.

reo-skjuvhastighet.back: How fast a material is deformed in shear, $\dot{\gamma} = \dfrac{d\gamma}{dt}$. In simple shear between two plates a distance $h$ apart, where the upper plate moves with velocity $v$ and the lower one is stationary, $\dot{\gamma} = v/h$. The unit is 1/s. The shear rate is used instead of the shear strain as a measure of flow, since the strain grows without bound as long as the fluid flows.

reo-skjuvfortunning.back:
![Viscosity function of a polymer melt on a log-log plot with a zero-shear plateau, a shear-thinning region and a plateau at high shear rates](/kort/materialteknik/viskositetsfunktion.svg)

The decrease in the viscosity of a polymer melt as the shear rate increases. The reason is that the chains in the flow stretch, orient in the flow direction and disentangle (if the molecular weight is above the entanglement molecular weight), so that they offer less resistance to flow.

reo-svetslinje.back: The line in an injection molded part where two or more flow fronts meet, when the shape of the part causes the melt flow to split in the cavity. The weldline is a weak spot in the part, so careful consideration must be given to where it ends up. Too low an injection temperature can give weak weldlines.

reo-eftertryck.back: The pressure maintained on the melt in injection molding after the cavity has been filled, to counteract the shrinkage as the material solidifies. The holding pressure is maintained until the gate has solidified; thereafter the part continues to cool without increased pressure.

reo-shish-kebab.back: A special crystalline structure in semi-crystalline polymers, most commonly in isotactic polypropylene and polyethylene: a fibril nucleus (shish) alternating with lamellae of folded chains (kebab). It forms when the melt is sheared while it is simultaneously cooled, e.g. in injection molding, and gives considerably better mechanical properties than the corresponding equilibrium structure with spherulites.

reo-varfor-viskoelastisk-smalta.front: Why is a polymer melt viscoelastic?
reo-varfor-viskoelastisk-smalta.back:
- **Elastic component:** the chains can be stretched by the flow but have a preferred conformation that they return to when the flow stops. They thus store energy during the flow.
- **Viscous component:** the chains slide past each other, and the friction between the molecules gives the viscous resistance.

When the flow is stopped, the chains recover their preferred conformation but do not move back to their original positions. That is why the melt can flow.

reo-viskositetsfunktionens-omraden.front: Describe the viscosity function of a polymer melt and what the chains do in each region
reo-viskositetsfunktionens-omraden.back:
![Viscosity function of a polymer melt on a log-log plot with a zero-shear plateau, a shear-thinning region and a plateau at high shear rates](/kort/materialteknik/viskositetsfunktion.svg)

Viscosity versus shear rate on a log-log plot, with three regions:

1. **Zero-shear viscosity** (plateau at low shear rates): the stresses from the flow are of the same order of magnitude as the stresses from the thermal motion of the chains, so the chains maintain their preferred conformation. The level depends on the material, the molecular weight and the molecular weight distribution.
2. **Shear-thinning region:** the chains stretch, orient in the flow direction and disentangle, and the viscosity decreases with increasing shear rate.
3. **Infinite-shear viscosity** (plateau at very high shear rates, at a lower level than the zero-shear plateau): maximum stretching, orientation and disentanglement has been reached, and the viscosity no longer depends on the shear rate. It is very difficult to measure for melts and can be left out of a sketch.

reo-extruderns-zoner.front: What happens to the polymer in the three zones of a single screw extruder?
reo-extruderns-zoner.back:
![Single screw extruder with hopper, barrel, screw, die and the three zones](/kort/materialteknik/enskruvsextruder.svg)

The pellets are fed through the hopper into the barrel.

1. **Solids conveying zone:** the screw transports and compacts the pellets. The zone is often cooled so that the pellets do not melt and clog the inlet.
2. **Melting or transition zone:** in the heated part of the barrel the pellets melt and are homogenized.
3. **Metering zone:** the pressure is built up so that the melt is pushed through the die at the end of the extruder.

reo-formsprutningscykelns-steg.front: Describe the steps of the injection molding cycle in order
reo-formsprutningscykelns-steg.back:
1. The mold closes (this is where the cycle starts).
2. The injection unit moves forward and the melt is injected into the cavity via the sprue, runners and gate.
3. The cavity is filled and holding pressure is applied to counteract the shrinkage, until the gate has solidified.
4. The injection unit is retracted and the screw rotates and feeds the next shot forward.
5. The part is cooled in the mold until it is sufficiently rigid, then the mold opens and the part is ejected.

$t_{\text{cycle}} = t_{\text{closing}} + t_{\text{cooling}} + t_{\text{ejection}}$, where the cooling time is approximately 80% of the cycle time.

reo-kyltid-och-godstjocklek.front: How does the wall thickness affect the cycle time in injection molding, and why?
reo-kyltid-och-godstjocklek.back: The cooling time dominates the cycle (approximately 80%), and it increases approximately with the square of the wall thickness. Double the thickness thus gives approximately four times as long a cooling time and therefore a much longer cycle. The reason is the low thermal conductivity of the plastic (low thermal diffusivity), which means that the heat is conducted out of the part slowly.

reo-filmblasning.back: Film blowing is a secondary shaping operation after extrusion. The melt is pushed through an annular die (film blowing die) and forms a tube. Air is blown in through the center of the die and inflates the tube, which is simultaneously drawn, so that the wall thickness decreases considerably. The film is cooled by air from the outside and solidifies before it reaches the nip rollers. The nip rollers squeeze the film together so that the overpressure in the bubble is maintained, and pull the film in the axial direction. Finally, the film is wound up.

reo-sf-smalta-amorf.front: In the molten state all polymers are amorphous, even those that are semi-crystalline in the solid state.
reo-sf-smalta-amorf.back: True. Regardless of whether the polymer is amorphous or semi-crystalline in the solid state, in the melt it has a disordered, random molecular orientation, i.e. it is amorphous.
options: True
False

reo-sf-viskositet-temperatur.front: The viscosity of a polymer melt increases when the temperature is raised.
reo-sf-viskositet-temperatur.back: False. The viscosity decreases when the temperature is raised ($\eta \propto 1/T$ on the lecture slide); the viscosity curves for e.g. ABS, PC and PA6 lie lower the higher the temperature is.
options: True
False

reo-sf-viskositet-molekylvikt.front: All else being equal, a polymer melt with a higher molecular weight has a higher viscosity.
reo-sf-viskositet-molekylvikt.back: True. The viscosity increases with the molecular weight ($\eta \propto M_w$ on the lecture slide). Conversely, a lower molecular weight gives a lower viscosity, so that the material becomes easier to process. Fillers also increase the viscosity.
options: True
False

reo-sf-nollskjuv-orientering.front: At low shear rates, in the zero-shear region, the polymer chains are strongly oriented in the flow direction.
reo-sf-nollskjuv-orientering.back:
![Viscosity function of a polymer melt on a log-log plot with a zero-shear plateau, a shear-thinning region and a plateau at high shear rates](/kort/materialteknik/viskositetsfunktion.svg)

False. At small or slow deformations the thermal motion of the chains has time to restore their preferred conformation, so the orientation does not change and the viscosity is constant. The chains become oriented only at higher shear rates, in the shear-thinning region.
options: True
False

reo-sf-delkristallin-krymper-mer.front: Semi-crystalline thermoplastics shrink more than amorphous ones when they solidify.
reo-sf-delkristallin-krymper-mer.back:
![p-V-T diagram: amorphous polymer with a change in slope at Tg and semi-crystalline polymer with a jump at Tm](/kort/materialteknik/pvt-amorf-delkristallin.svg)

True. Amorphous thermoplastics densify the least on solidification, since the chains cannot organize into regular, densely packed crystals. Semi-crystalline polymers shrink more; in injection molding this is partially counteracted by longer packing times and higher pressure.
options: True
False

reo-sf-snabbkylning-kristallinitet.front: Faster cooling gives a higher degree of crystallinity in a semi-crystalline polymer.
reo-sf-snabbkylning-kristallinitet.back: False. Rapid cooling lowers the crystallinity, since the microstructure is frozen before the chains have had time to organize completely into crystals.
options: True
False

reo-alt-produkt-extrudering.front: Which products are typically manufactured by extrusion, with or without secondary shaping?
reo-alt-produkt-extrudering.back: Extrusion gives products with a certain cross-sectional profile, e.g. pipes, tubes, filaments, profiles and films; with film casting or film blowing it becomes thin film. The push button of a ballpoint pen is injection molded (exam 2016-10), and mass-produced parts with complex shapes are exactly what injection molding is suited for.
options: Pipes
Thin packaging film
The push button of a ballpoint pen
Mass-produced parts with complex three-dimensional shapes

reo-alt-processfonster.front: Which pairs of processing defect and cause are correct for injection molding?
reo-alt-processfonster.back: The molding diagram is bounded by the melt temperature and the holding pressure. Too low a temperature gives short shots and weak weldlines, too high a temperature gives thermal degradation. Too low a holding pressure gives too much shrinkage, too high a holding pressure gives flash: the pressure in the cavity exceeds the clamping force and melt is forced out at the parting line of the mold.
options: Too low a melt temperature gives a short shot (unfilled cavity).
Too high a holding pressure gives flash.
Too low a melt temperature gives thermal degradation.
Too low a holding pressure gives flash.

reo-alt-formens-kanaler.front: Which statements about the channels of the injection mold are correct?
reo-alt-formens-kanaler.back: The melt flows from the barrel through the sprue and is distributed via the runners to the gates, which lead into the cavities. The gate is a small opening compared to the part and the runners and therefore solidifies before the part. If the mold has only one cavity, the sprue itself acts as the gate (sprue gate).
options: The sprue connects the barrel to the mold.
The runners distribute the melt to the cavities via the gates.
The gate is the largest channel of the mold and therefore solidifies last.
If the mold has only one cavity, no sprue is needed.

reo-viskositet-omrade-skjuvfortunnande.front: Which region of the viscosity function is the shear-thinning one? ![Viscosity versus shear rate on a log-log plot, divided into regions A, B and C from low to high shear rate](/kort/materialteknik/viskositetsfunktion-fraga.svg)
reo-viskositet-omrade-skjuvfortunnande.back:
![Viscosity function of a polymer melt on a log-log plot with a zero-shear plateau, a shear-thinning region and a plateau at high shear rates](/kort/materialteknik/viskositetsfunktion.svg)

B is the shear-thinning region, where the viscosity decreases with increasing shear rate because the chains stretch, orient in the flow direction and disentangle. A is the zero-shear viscosity, a plateau at low shear rates, and C is the infinite-shear viscosity, a plateau at very high shear rates that is difficult to measure for melts.
options: B
A
C

reo-viskositet-omrade-nollskjuv.front: Which region of the viscosity function corresponds to the zero-shear viscosity $\eta_0$? ![Viscosity versus shear rate on a log-log plot, divided into regions A, B and C from low to high shear rate](/kort/materialteknik/viskositetsfunktion-fraga.svg)
reo-viskositet-omrade-nollskjuv.back:
![Viscosity function of a polymer melt on a log-log plot with a zero-shear plateau, a shear-thinning region and a plateau at high shear rates](/kort/materialteknik/viskositetsfunktion.svg)

The zero-shear viscosity is the plateau at low shear rates (A). There, the stresses from the flow are of the same order of magnitude as the stresses from the thermal motion of the chains, so the chains maintain their preferred conformation and the viscosity is constant. The level depends on the material, the molecular weight and the molecular weight distribution.
options: A
B
C

reo-extruder-smaltzon.front: In which zone of a single screw extruder do the pellets melt?
reo-extruder-smaltzon.back:
![Single screw extruder with hopper, barrel, screw, die and the three zones](/kort/materialteknik/enskruvsextruder.svg)

The pellets melt and are homogenized in the melting or transition zone, in the heated part of the barrel. The solids conveying zone transports and compacts the pellets and is often cooled so that they do not melt and clog the inlet. In the metering zone the pressure is built up that pushes the melt through the die.
options: The melting or transition zone
The solids conveying zone
The metering zone
In the hopper, before the pellets reach the screw

reo-pvt-sprang.front: In a p-V-T diagram the curve makes a jump in specific volume at a certain temperature. Which type of polymer and which temperature does this apply to?
reo-pvt-sprang.back:
![p-V-T diagram: amorphous polymer with a change in slope at Tg and semi-crystalline polymer with a jump at Tm](/kort/materialteknik/pvt-amorf-delkristallin.svg)

For a semi-crystalline polymer the specific volume drops in a jump at $T_m$ when crystallization begins during cooling. An amorphous polymer has no jump, only a change in slope at $T_g$, where the slope of the curve changes from that of the melt to that of the glass.
options: A semi-crystalline polymer, at the melting temperature $T_m$
An amorphous polymer, at the glass transition temperature $T_g$
An amorphous polymer, at the melting temperature $T_m$
A semi-crystalline polymer, at the glass transition temperature $T_g$

reo-formsprutning-produkt-ingotssystem.front: When the mold opens after an injection molding shot, a single connected piece of plastic is ejected. Which parts of the piece are the sprue and runner system, which is separated from the product?
reo-formsprutning-produkt-ingotssystem.back: The melt flows from the barrel through the sprue, is distributed in the runners and is led via small gates into the cavities, where the parts get their shape. The plastic in the sprue, runners and gates also solidifies and comes out, but it is only the way in; the product is the parts from the cavities. The ejector pins belong to the mold and eject the piece; they do not come out with it.
options: The plastic that has solidified in the sprue
The plastic that has solidified in the runners
The gates
The parts that have been formed in the cavities
The ejector pins

reo-formsprutningsmaskinens-enheter-uppg.front: What are the four main units of an injection molding machine, and what does each one do?
reo-formsprutningsmaskinens-enheter-uppg.back:
* **Plasticizing unit:** a form of single screw extruder. The pellets are fed from the hopper into the heated cylinder, where the rotating screw melts them (heat conduction from the cylinder and heat from friction and flow) and collects a predetermined amount of melt in front of the screw tip.
* **Injection unit:** moves forward and pushes the melt into the mold at high pressure and high speed; holding pressure is then applied.
* **Mold:** sprue, runners, gate and cavity, cooling system (sometimes) and ejectors. The part is cooled in the mold until it is rigid enough to be ejected.
* **Clamping unit:** closes the mold and keeps it closed against the pressure in the cavity. If the pressure in the cavity becomes too high relative to the clamping force of the machine, melt is forced out at the parting line of the mold (flash).

reo-sf-total-kyltid-eftertryck.front: In injection molding, the part starts to solidify only once the holding pressure has been released.
reo-sf-total-kyltid-eftertryck.back: False. The melt starts to solidify against the relatively cold mold already while the holding pressure is applied; the holding pressure counteracts the shrinkage and is maintained until the gate has solidified. Thereafter the solidification continues without increased pressure until the part is sufficiently rigid to be ejected. The total cooling time thus includes both the time with holding pressure and the time after it, and it accounts for approximately 80% of the cycle time.
options: True
False

reo-sf-tryck-hojer-tg-tm.front: High pressure during processing raises the glass transition temperature of an amorphous thermoplastic.
reo-sf-tryck-hojer-tg-tm.back: True. High pressure pushes the molecules closer together, so more thermal energy is required to free them so that they can flow. In a p-V-T diagram the change in slope at Tg (amorphous thermoplastics) and the jump at Tm (semi-crystalline thermoplastics) are therefore shifted to higher temperatures as the pressure increases.
options: True
False

quiz-creep-krypning.front: What is true about creep in polymers?
quiz-creep-krypning.back: In a creep test the stress is kept constant and the strain is measured over time. Constant strain with measured stress is instead a stress relaxation test. Cutting sections through the creep curves at constant time gives isochronous stress-strain curves. Impact tests are short-term tests, in which polymers can most often be considered purely elastic, whereas creep tests are long-term tests.
options: A creep test is performed at constant strain
A creep test is performed at constant stress
Creep curves can be used to construct isochronous diagrams
Creep is a measure of impact performance

polymer-krackelering-vad-stammer.front: What is true about crazing in an amorphous polymer?
polymer-krackelering-vad-stammer.back: Crazes are microcracks that form perpendicular to the maximum principal stress, starting at stress concentrations such as scratches, dust particles or material inhomogeneities. They impair clarity and reflect light, which makes them clearly visible in transparent materials.
options: The crazes form in planes perpendicular to the maximum principal stress
The crazes are nucleated at stress concentrations such as scratches and dust particles
The crazes form in planes parallel to the maximum principal stress
The crazes do not affect the clarity of the material

polymer-duktilt-brott-ordning.front: In what order do the events occur when a semi-crystalline thermoplastic, e.g. PP, is drawn to failure at room temperature?
polymer-duktilt-brott-ordning.back: First the deformation is linearly elastic and reversible (for PP up to approx. 0.5 %). Then the curve becomes nonlinear as microcracks form at the interfaces between the spherulites, which become visible as stress whitening. At the stress maximum the yield point is reached, the stress drops and necking follows, with a long cold drawing in which the spherulitic structure is deformed and broken up. A linear region, crazing and brittle fracture at approx. 1 % strain instead describe an amorphous thermoplastic below Tg.
options: Linearly elastic region, microcracks between the spherulites (stress whitening), yield point, necking and cold drawing
Necking, stress whitening, linearly elastic region, yield point
Linearly elastic region, crazing, brittle fracture at approx. 1 % strain
Cold drawing, yield point, linearly elastic region, stress whitening

polymer-stress-whitening-var.front: Where do the microcracks that cause stress whitening form in a semi-crystalline polymer?
polymer-stress-whitening-var.back: The spherulites are the largest lengthscale in a semi-crystalline polymer, and the largest lengthscale fails first. The microcracks therefore form at the interfaces between the spherulites and become roughly as long as the spherulites. When they become visible they are called stress whitening. Crosslink points do not exist in a thermoplastic.
options: At the interfaces between the spherulites
Inside the individual crystalline lamellae
Along the covalent bonds of the backbone
At the crosslink points between the chains

polymer-isokrona-kurvor-konstruktion.front: How are isochronous stress-strain curves constructed from creep data?
polymer-isokrona-kurvor-konstruktion.back: Isochronous means "same time": each curve applies to a given time of loading, e.g. 1 day or 1 year. Sections at constant strain with the stress against time instead give isometric curves. Impact tests are short-term tests and give no creep data.
options: By cutting sections through the creep curves at constant time, with the stress plotted against the strain
By cutting sections through the creep curves at constant strain, with the stress plotted against time
By cutting sections at constant stress, with the strain plotted against temperature
By impact tests at different temperatures
