polymer-kryp-rent-viskost-svar.front: What response does a purely viscous fluid give in a creep test at constant stress σ₀?
polymer-kryp-rent-viskost-svar.back: A purely viscous fluid obeys Newton's law of viscosity, so the strain becomes $\gamma(t) = \dfrac{\sigma_0}{\eta}\,t$. An instantaneous strain that then stays constant is the purely elastic response (Hooke). An initial elastic response that then tends to an asymptote is the solid-like viscoelastic response.
options: The strain increases linearly with time, with the slope σ₀/η
An instantaneous strain that then stays constant
An instantaneous elastic strain that then approaches an asymptote
No strain at all

polymer-kryp-aterhamtning.front: What happens when the creep stress is removed from a viscoelastic material (recovery)?
polymer-kryp-aterhamtning.back: The strain that is recovered (the recovery strain) shows how much elastic energy was stored in the structure. The rest is not recovered, because chains that have slid past each other remain in their new positions; this is the viscous loss. That all of the strain is recovered applies only to a purely elastic material.
options: Part of the strain is recovered quickly, but a residual strain remains
All of the strain is recovered immediately
The strain continues to increase at the same rate as during loading
The strain becomes negative

polymer-var-star-polymerer-ut.front: Where do polymeric materials stand out?
polymer-var-star-polymerer-ut.back: Polymers and polymer composites have good mechanical properties with respect to density and are therefore key to lightweight design. Because they are viscoelastic, part of the vibration is converted into viscous losses, which gives damping. They are also thermally and electrically insulating; electrical conductivity requires conductive fillers. Compared with metals, polymers withstand lower temperatures, and the service temperature is one of the most important criteria when selecting a polymer.
options: Lightweight design (high mechanical properties with respect to density)
Vibration damping
High service temperature
High electrical conductivity without additives

polymer-krazer-langsam-deformation.front: At high strain rates the crazes become large and form early during loading.
polymer-krazer-langsam-deformation.back: It is the other way round. Crazing depends on the strain rate: at high strain rates the crazes are small and form shortly before failure, or not at all. At slow deformation they become large and appear early during loading.
options: True
False

polymer-krazer-fibriller.front: Crazes are less dangerous than actual cracks, because the craze boundaries are held together by load bearing fibrils.
polymer-krazer-fibriller.back: The crazes are connected by load bearing fibrils and are therefore less dangerous than actual cracks. They are nevertheless a visible warning: in transparent parts they are visible because they impair clarity and reflect light.
options: True
False

polymer-isometriska-kurvor.front: Isometric curves are obtained by cutting sections through the creep curves at constant time, with the stress plotted against the strain.
polymer-isometriska-kurvor.back: That describes isochronous curves ("same time"). Isometric curves ("same strain") are obtained by cutting sections through the creep curves at constant strain, with the stress plotted against time. They resemble the result of a stress relaxation test.
options: True
False

polymer-elastomer-reversibel.front: The deformation of a crosslinked elastomer is reversible as long as no crosslinks are broken.
polymer-elastomer-reversibel.back: The crosslinks enable an elastomer to withstand very large deformations (rubber elasticity). Since elastomers are only weakly crosslinked, large parts of the chains can be stretched out, and the deformation is reversed as long as the crosslinks are intact.
options: True
False

polymer-sprott-over-tg-kryp-utmattning.front: Brittle fracture of polymers can occur even above Tg, in creep rupture and fatigue.
polymer-sprott-over-tg-kryp-utmattning.back: Brittle fracture in a short-term tensile test applies to thermoplastics below Tg and highly crosslinked polymers. In creep rupture and fatigue tests, brittle fracture can occur even at temperatures above Tg.
options: True
False

polymer-slagprov-elastiskt-langtid-visko.front: In impact tests polymers can most often be considered purely elastic, whereas in long-term tests such as creep tests they behave viscoelastically.
polymer-slagprov-elastiskt-langtid-visko.back: The behavior of polymers is time-dependent. At short timescales (impact tests) they generally behave as purely elastic materials, at long timescales (creep) the behavior is clearly viscoelastic. The most difficult to assess are timescales of the same order of magnitude as a standard tensile test.
options: True
False

polymer-begrepp-krypmodul.back: The applied constant stress divided by the time-dependent strain in a creep test: $E_c = \dfrac{\sigma_0}{\varepsilon(t)}$. The creep modulus thus decreases with time. In shear it corresponds to the shear creep modulus $G_c = \sigma_0/\gamma(t)$.

polymer-begrepp-deborahtal.back: The ratio between the characteristic material timescale and the observation timescale: $De = \dfrac{\text{material timescale}}{\text{observation time}}$. When De tends to 0 the material behaves as a purely viscous fluid, when De tends to infinity as a purely elastic solid. In between it is viscoelastic ("everything flows", compare the pitch drop experiment).

polymer-begrepp-halsbildning.back: A localized reduction in cross-sectional area that follows the yield point when a semi-crystalline polymer is drawn. It is followed by a long cold drawing in which the spherulitic structure is first deformed and then broken up, so that highly oriented regions are formed.

polymer-halsbildning-molekylmodell.front: Describe what happens in the molecular structure during necking in a semi-crystalline polymer.
polymer-halsbildning-molekylmodell.back:
During necking and cold drawing the spherulitic structure is deformed and broken up, so that highly oriented regions are formed. The molecular model includes:

- The amorphous ties between the lamellae are completely extended, which makes the lamellae slip and tilt relative to each other (slip-tilt).
- On further drawing, lamellae fragments get aligned in the direction of draw and form fibrils of alternating crystal blocks and stretched amorphous regions.

polymer-isokront-diagram-dimensionering.front: How is an isochronous stress-strain diagram used when dimensioning a plastic part?
polymer-isokront-diagram-dimensionering.back: Each isochronous curve applies to a given time of loading, and the diagram applies to the temperature at which the creep tests were performed. Choose the curve for the service life of the product, e.g. 1 year. Enter with the stress on the y-axis and read off the strain the part has reached after creep during that time; compare with the allowable strain. Conversely, a maximum allowable strain gives the maximum allowable stress.

polymer-begrepp-boltzmann-superposition.back:
In linear viscoelasticity the deformation is the sum of the strains that each load change gives rise to, independently of the loads already acting. For stepwise stress changes $\Delta\sigma_i$ at the times $t_i$ the strain becomes

$\varepsilon(t) = \sum_i \Delta\sigma_i\,J(t - t_i)$,

where $J$ is the creep compliance. Each step contributes according to how long it has been acting, so the strain depends on the entire loading history and not only on the stress acting at this moment. The principle holds as long as the polymer behaves linearly viscoelastically.

polymer-boltzmann-tvastegs.front: A polymer has the creep compliance $J(t)$. The stress $\sigma_0$ is applied at $t = 0$ and raised to $2\sigma_0$ at $t_1$. Which expression gives the strain at $t > t_1$ (linear viscoelasticity)?
polymer-boltzmann-tvastegs.back: According to the Boltzmann Superposition Principle, the contribution from each stress step is added, counted from the time at which the step was applied: $\varepsilon(t) = \sigma_0 J(t) + (2\sigma_0 - \sigma_0)\,J(t - t_1)$. The second step is only the increase $\sigma_0$, and it has been acting for a shorter time. $2\sigma_0 J(t)$ applies if the whole stress had been applied already at $t = 0$; since $J$ increases with time, that strain becomes larger.
options: $\sigma_0 J(t) + \sigma_0 J(t - t_1)$
$2\sigma_0 J(t)$
$2\sigma_0 J(t - t_1)$
$\sigma_0 J(t) + 2\sigma_0 J(t - t_1)$

polymer-smalta-kryp-aterhamtning.front: A polymer melt and a solid polymer are each loaded in a creep test (constant stress, linear viscoelastic region). What distinguishes the strain curve of the melt from that of the solid polymer?
polymer-smalta-kryp-aterhamtning.back: A polymer melt is dominated by the viscous component, since the chains in the molten state easily slide past each other: it behaves liquid-like (Maxwell model), and after the initial elastic response the strain increases linearly with the slope $\sigma_0/\eta$. A solid polymer is dominated by the elastic component, since the chains are trapped by other chains: it behaves solid-like (Kelvin-Voigt), and the strain tends to an asymptote. Both have an initial elastic response, and in both cases part of the strain is quickly recovered after unloading, but not all of it; chains that have slid past each other remain in their new positions.
options: The strain of the melt continues to increase linearly with time, whereas the strain of the solid polymer approaches an asymptote.
The melt has no elastic component, so none of the strain is recovered when the load is removed.
The strain of the solid polymer is always fully recovered when the load is removed, that of the melt is not.
The strain of the melt is constant during the entire loading, since the melt is a liquid.

polymer-dragkurvor-fyra-typer.front: Describe the typical stress-strain curve at room temperature for an amorphous thermoplastic, a semi-crystalline thermoplastic, a thermoset and an elastomer.
polymer-dragkurvor-fyra-typer.back:
* **Amorphous thermoplastic** (Tg usually above room temperature, e.g. PS and PMMA): stiff and brittle. The curve is linear and the deformation reversible until small microcracks (crazes) form shortly before failure; the curve then becomes nonlinear. Exception: PC is very impact resistant although it is amorphous.
* **Semi-crystalline thermoplastic** (between Tg and Tm, e.g. PP and PE): linearly elastic region, then nonlinear with stress whitening, yield point and drop in stress, necking and long cold drawing; ductile failure at large strain.
* **Thermoset** (highly crosslinked, e.g. epoxy): high stiffness and low strain at failure, brittle fracture.
* **Elastomer** (weakly crosslinked, used above its Tg): very low stiffness and very high strain at failure; withstands large deformations that are reversed.

Below their Tg, polymers generally fail by brittle fracture in a short-term tensile test, semi-crystalline ones included.

polymer-dragkurva-kalldragning-typ.front: At room temperature a polymer in a tensile test shows a clear yield point, followed by a drop in stress, necking and a long cold drawing to very large strain. What type of polymer is it most likely?
polymer-dragkurva-kalldragning-typ.back: Ductile failure with stress whitening, yield point, necking and cold drawing occurs in semi-crystalline polymers between Tg and Tm; for semi-crystalline plastics Tg is usually below room temperature. An amorphous thermoplastic below Tg and a thermoset fail by brittle fracture at small strain. An elastomer has very low stiffness and large, reversible strain instead of cold drawing.
options: A semi-crystalline thermoplastic, e.g. PP or PE
An amorphous thermoplastic below its Tg, e.g. PS
A thermoset, e.g. epoxy
A crosslinked elastomer

polymer-krypmodul-ur-isokron-kurva.front: A plastic part is loaded with a constant stress of 4 MPa for one year. The 1-year isochronous curve then gives a strain of 0.8 %. Which Young's modulus (creep modulus) should be used in e.g. a deflection calculation?
polymer-krypmodul-ur-isokron-kurva.back: The creep modulus is $E_c = \sigma_0/\varepsilon(t) = 4\ \text{MPa}/0.008 = 500$ MPa $= 0.5$ GPa. It applies only to that time of loading and temperature and is inserted into Hooke's law or the beam formula instead of the short-term modulus. 5 GPa is obtained if 0.8 % is taken as 0.0008 and 50 GPa if the strain is taken as 0.00008; 32 kPa is obtained if the stress is multiplied by the strain.
options: 0.5 GPa
5 GPa
50 GPa
32 kPa

polymer-dimensionering-isokron-tvarsnitt.front: A plastic rod is to carry a tensile force of 600 N for one year without the strain exceeding 1 %. The 1-year isochronous curve gives 12 MPa at 1 % strain. What is the minimum cross-sectional area?
polymer-dimensionering-isokron-tvarsnitt.back: The method: choose the isochronous curve for the service life of the product, read off the allowable stress at the allowable strain and calculate the area. Here $A = F/\sigma = 600\ \text{N}/12\ \text{N/mm}^2 = 50$ mm². 5 and 500 mm² are errors in the power of ten, and 7 200 mm² is obtained if the force is multiplied by the stress. A longer service life gives a lower curve and requires a larger area.
options: 50 mm²
5 mm²
500 mm²
7 200 mm²

polymer-presspassning-relaxation.front: A tubular plastic feature is pressed on a metal stud so that the strain in the tube is kept constant. How does the stress in the tube, and thereby the force required to disassemble the parts, change with time?
polymer-presspassning-relaxation.back: An imposed constant strain is a relaxation case. One calculates the strain (the change in diameter divided by the diameter), follows the isometric curve (constant strain) from the creep data and reads off the stress at different times, e.g. directly after assembly and after one year. The hoop stress gives the pressure against the stud, and the force to disassemble the parts is the friction against the stud, so it decreases as the stress relaxes. Constant stress with increasing strain is instead a creep case.
options: The stress decreases with time (stress relaxation), so the force becomes smaller; it is read off along an isometric curve at the strain in question.
The stress increases with time, because the material creeps.
The stress is constant, because the strain is constant.
The strain increases while the stress is constant.
